meta.blurb: Eight years ago, Anne Elliot let her family talk her out of the man she loved. Now Captain Wentworth is back, richer, prouder and coldly polite. She must sit across the room and watch him look at other women.
meta.bible: Sir Walter Elliot: a vain baronet of Kellynch Hall in Somerset; loves his looks and his rank; spends too much money. Elizabeth Elliot: his eldest daughter, handsome, cold and proud. Anne Elliot: his middle daughter, 27, gentle, wise and often overlooked; the heroine. Mary Musgrove: his youngest daughter, who is married and always complains of her health. Charles Musgrove: Mary's good-natured husband, who lives at Uppercross. Lady Russell: a wise older friend of the family and Anne's godmother figure; she persuaded Anne eight years ago. Mr Shepherd: Sir Walter's lawyer. Admiral Croft: a cheerful naval officer who rents Kellynch Hall. Mrs Croft: the Admiral's wife, Sophia, who is Captain Wentworth's sister. Frederick Wentworth: a naval officer; poor when Anne first loved him, now a rich and respected Captain. Mr and Mrs Musgrove: Charles's parents, kind and simple, of Uppercross Hall. Louisa Musgrove and Henrietta Musgrove: Charles's lively sisters. Charles Hayter: Henrietta's cousin and sweetheart, a young clergyman. Captain Harville: a naval officer living at Lyme, lame from a wound. Captain Benwick: a sad, bookish officer whose fiancee Fanny Harville has died. Mr William Elliot: Sir Walter's cousin and heir, charming but selfish. Mrs Clay: Mr Shepherd's daughter, a friend of Elizabeth who wants to marry Sir Walter. Mrs Smith: Anne's old school friend, now poor, ill and a widow in Bath. Places: Kellynch Hall; Somerset; Uppercross; Winthrop; Lyme; the Cobb, the long stone sea wall at Lyme; Bath; Camden Place; the Octagon Room, where the concert is held; the White Hart, an inn in Bath; Westgate Buildings. Time: 1814, just after the long war with France. Voice and tone: gentle, witty and tender; Anne's feelings are quiet and deep; the second chance is earned, never rushed. More names and places: Lady Elliot: Sir Walter's late wife, who died fourteen years ago. Walter and Charles: Mary's two small sons. Dick Musgrove: the Musgroves' dead son, a poor sailor. Mrs Harville: Captain Harville's wife. Fanny Harville: Captain Harville's sister, Benwick's fiancee, who died. Lady Dalrymple: a grand cousin of the Elliots, a widowed viscountess in Laura Place, Bath. Miss Carteret: her daughter. Mr Smith: Mrs Smith's late husband. Mrs Rooke: Mrs Smith's kind nurse. Admiral Baldwin: a weathered naval man Sir Walter dislikes. Edward Wentworth: Frederick's older brother, once the curate at Monkford. Monkford: the village near Kellynch where Anne met Frederick. Kellynch Lodge: Lady Russell's house. Milsom Street and Molland's, a shop where Anne meets Wentworth. Rivers Street: where Lady Russell stays in Bath. The Laconia and the Asp: Wentworth's ships. The Cobb at Lyme. The West Indies: where Mr Smith owned property. Mr Elliot's hidden aim: to keep Mrs Clay from becoming Lady Elliot.
chapters: A Favourite at the Great House

beats.scene: Sir Walter Elliot reads his own family's page in a thick book
beats.summary: Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall is a vain man who loves reading about himself.

beats.scene: Sir Walter stands in a long hall beside a portrait of his late wife
beats.summary: Sir Walter's wife died fourteen years ago, and he has three daughters.

beats.scene: Elizabeth sits very straight at a long table in a grand dining room
beats.summary: Elizabeth, the eldest, is handsome and proud, and she runs the house like her father.

beats.scene: Anne Elliot sits quietly in the corner of the room, reading
beats.summary: Anne, the middle daughter, is gentle and wise, and her own family overlooks her.

beats.scene: Mary Elliot takes leave of her father in the hall on her wedding day
beats.summary: The youngest daughter, Mary, has married Charles Musgrove and lives at Uppercross.

beats.scene: Lady Russell listens carefully to Anne in the sitting room at Kellynch Lodge
beats.summary: Lady Russell, the family's close friend, is the one person who values Anne.

beats.scene: Sir Walter studies a heap of bills with a frown at his desk
beats.summary: Sir Walter has spent far too much money, and his debts keep growing.

beats.scene: Mr Shepherd, a careful lawyer, bows politely to Sir Walter in the study
beats.summary: Mr Shepherd, Sir Walter's lawyer, is afraid to say how bad the money trouble is.

beats.scene: Lady Russell lays a plan of savings before a frowning Sir Walter
beats.summary: Lady Russell asks Sir Walter to save money, but he cannot bear to give up anything.

beats.scene: Mr Shepherd points to a map and suggests moving to Bath
beats.summary: Mr Shepherd suggests renting Kellynch Hall and moving to Bath, and Sir Walter agrees.

beats.scene: Mr Shepherd speaks eagerly to Sir Walter, holding a letter
beats.summary: Mr Shepherd says a rich naval officer, Admiral Croft, wants to rent a house in Somerset.

beats.scene: Sir Walter wrinkles his nose as if he smells something unpleasant
beats.summary: Sir Walter dislikes the navy because it raises low-born men and spoils their looks.

beats.scene: Sir Walter describes an old admiral with a brown, wrinkled face
beats.summary: Sir Walter complains that Admiral Baldwin looked sixty because of the sea.

beats.scene: Mr Shepherd counts the good points of a naval tenant on his fingers
beats.summary: Mr Shepherd argues that an admiral would pay well, keep the house, and honour Sir Walter.

beats.scene: Mr Shepherd mentions a name from the past while Anne sits very still
beats.summary: Mr Shepherd adds that the admiral's wife has a brother who was once a curate near Kellynch, a Mr Wentworth.

beats.scene: Anne turns her face away toward the window while the men talk
beats.summary: Sir Walter does not remember Wentworth, but Anne knows the name too well.

beats.scene: Anne walks alone beneath tall trees in the grounds of Kellynch
beats.summary: That evening Anne walks in the grounds and remembers the summer eight years ago.

beats.scene: Anne and the young Wentworth talk together on a bench by a river
beats.summary: Frederick Wentworth was clever, bright and sure of himself, and he and Anne fell deeply in love.

beats.scene: Sir Walter shakes his head coldly and turns his back
beats.summary: Sir Walter coldly refuses to help the engagement, which he thinks beneath his daughter.

beats.scene: Lady Russell speaks gravely to Anne in a quiet drawing room
beats.summary: Lady Russell, afraid for Anne, persuades her to end the engagement, and Wentworth leaves in anger.

beats.scene: A young officer stands at the rail of a ship leaving the harbour
beats.summary: Wentworth sails away in anger, and Anne is left with a broken heart.

beats.scene: Wentworth in a naval coat stands proudly on the deck of a warship
beats.summary: Wentworth rises quickly in the navy, takes enemy ships and becomes a rich captain.

beats.scene: Anne looks at her faded face in a small mirror
beats.summary: Anne's bloom fades in the years of sorrow, and Sir Walter says she has grown thin and plain.

beats.scene: Charles Musgrove asks Anne a question while she stands by a window
beats.summary: At twenty-two Anne refused a good offer of marriage from Charles Musgrove, who then married Mary.

beats.scene: Anne and Lady Russell sit by the fire in quiet talk
beats.summary: Anne still thinks Lady Russell's advice was right, though it cost her everything she loved.

beats.scene: Admiral Croft, a tall weathered man, bows to Sir Walter in the hall
beats.summary: The cheerful Admiral Croft comes to see Kellynch Hall, and Sir Walter is surprised to like him.

beats.scene: Admiral Croft points at the many looking-glasses in a dressing room
beats.summary: The Admiral laughs at the mirrors in Sir Walter's dressing room, and the mirrors are put away.

beats.scene: Mrs Croft, a sunburnt woman, talks plainly with Anne in the garden
beats.summary: Mrs Croft, who is direct and kind, tells Anne she has sailed with her husband and that her brother is Captain Wentworth.

beats.scene: Sir Walter signs a paper at the table while the Admiral watches
beats.summary: The Admiral agrees to rent Kellynch Hall, and the lease is signed at last.

beats.scene: Anne waves goodbye as the family carriage leaves Kellynch Hall
beats.summary: Sir Walter and Elizabeth leave for Bath, and Anne stays behind with Lady Russell.

beats.scene: Anne arrives by carriage at a low thatched cottage near a large house
beats.summary: Anne goes to her sister Mary's small house at Uppercross for a long stay.

beats.scene: Mary lies on a sofa with a hand to her forehead, looking miserable
beats.summary: Mary greets Anne from the sofa with complaints and says nobody cares about her health.

beats.scene: Two small boys roll noisily on the floor while Mary tries to speak
beats.summary: Mary's two small sons are noisy and spoiled, and she cannot control them.

beats.scene: Mr and Mrs Musgrove sit in a warm old-fashioned room at the Great House
beats.summary: The elder Musgroves are warm, simple, old-fashioned people at the Great House.

beats.scene: Louisa and Henrietta Musgrove laugh together over a new piece of music
beats.summary: The two Musgrove daughters, Louisa and Henrietta, are young, pretty and high-spirited.

beats.scene: Henrietta sits beside a young clergyman at the Great House dinner table
beats.summary: Henrietta is fond of her cousin Charles Hayter, a young clergyman with poor prospects.

beats.scene: Anne plays the piano in a lit room while the others dance
beats.summary: Anne plays the piano for the young people's dances and is content to sit in a corner.

beats.scene: Anne stands between Mary and Mrs Musgrove as they argue in a parlour
beats.summary: Mary and Mrs Musgrove quarrel over small things, and Anne quietly soothes both of them.

beats.scene: Mrs Musgrove wipes her eyes beside a portrait of a young sailor
beats.summary: Mrs Musgrove tells Anne about her son Dick, a wild sailor who died at sea.

beats.scene: A letter in Charles Musgrove's hand, and Anne looks up in alarm
beats.summary: Charles hears that Captain Wentworth will soon visit the Crofts at Kellynch, and Anne is alarmed.

beats.scene: Anne sits alone in lamplight with her sewing forgotten in her lap
beats.summary: Anne knows she must soon meet Wentworth again, and she tries to calm herself.

beats.scene: Anne looks out at a grey sky and tries to reason with herself
beats.summary: Anne tells herself that time changes everyone and he has surely forgotten her.

beats.scene: Charles Musgrove tells Mary about meeting Wentworth at Kellynch
beats.summary: Charles meets Wentworth at Kellynch, likes him at once and asks him to visit Uppercross.

beats.scene: Footsteps approach the door of the cottage and Anne rises slowly
beats.summary: The next morning Anne hears Wentworth's voice outside the cottage door.

beats.scene: Anne and Captain Wentworth bow stiffly in the Musgroves' parlour
beats.summary: Anne and Wentworth meet again after eight years, and he is polite and cold.

beats.scene: Wentworth talks easily with Mary while Anne sits quietly beside them
beats.summary: Wentworth speaks freely to Mary and Charles but gives Anne only cool good manners.

beats.scene: Anne stands behind a half-open door and listens to voices in the next room
beats.summary: Anne overhears that Wentworth thinks she is so changed he would hardly have known her.

beats.scene: Anne presses her hands together and breathes slowly beside a window
beats.summary: Anne is deeply wounded, but she tells herself it is only the truth.

beats.scene: Wentworth sits at the Great House dinner table between Louisa and Henrietta
beats.summary: At dinner at the Great House Wentworth talks and laughs with the Musgrove sisters.

beats.scene: Anne walks home alone through a dark lane under autumn trees
beats.summary: Anne walks home and tells herself that Wentworth is nothing to her now.

beats.scene: Wentworth rides up the lane to the Great House on a bright morning
beats.summary: Wentworth visits Uppercross almost every day, and the Musgroves quickly love him.

beats.scene: Wentworth tells a story at the dinner table while everyone listens
beats.summary: Wentworth tells exciting sea stories at dinner, and everyone listens, including Anne.

beats.scene: Mrs Musgrove tells Wentworth about her lost son beside the fire
beats.summary: Mrs Musgrove tells Wentworth about her son Dick, who served under him, and Wentworth is gentle.

beats.scene: Wentworth laughs with the Musgrove sisters in a sunny parlour
beats.summary: Wentworth says he wants to marry a pleasant, strong-minded woman, and the Musgrove sisters listen.

beats.scene: Anne plays the piano while Wentworth dances with Louisa in a bright room
beats.summary: Anne plays for the dancing again, and Wentworth thanks her with cold courtesy.

beats.scene: Charles Hayter bows stiffly in the doorway as Henrietta looks away
beats.summary: Charles Hayter returns and finds Henrietta cool, because Wentworth has turned her head.

beats.scene: A small boy lies pale on a sofa while a doctor bends over him
beats.summary: Mary's elder boy falls and dislocates his collarbone, and Anne stays to nurse him.

beats.scene: Mary glares at Charles as he puts on his coat for dinner
beats.summary: Charles goes to a dinner at the Great House, while Mary complains and Anne stays with the boy.

beats.scene: Little Walter climbs onto Anne's back while she kneels by the sofa
beats.summary: The next day Walter climbs on Anne's back and cannot be shaken off.

beats.scene: Wentworth lifts the boy from Anne's back and sets him on the floor
beats.summary: Wentworth quietly lifts the boy away and leaves before Anne can thank him.

beats.scene: A party of walkers sets out on a country path in autumn sunlight
beats.summary: The young people plan a long walk to Winthrop on a fine autumn day, and Anne joins them.

beats.scene: Anne walks slowly behind the others past golden leaves and brown fields
beats.summary: Anne walks behind the party and enjoys the quiet of the autumn countryside.

beats.scene: The party eats nuts under a hedge in the autumn sun
beats.summary: The party stops to gather nuts, and Anne sits behind the hedge, out of sight.

beats.scene: Wentworth holds a glossy nut and speaks earnestly to Louisa
beats.summary: Anne overhears Wentworth tell Louisa that a firm mind is like a nut that stays whole.

beats.scene: Louisa raises her chin proudly while Wentworth smiles beside her
beats.summary: Louisa says she would never be persuaded to do something she thought wrong, and Wentworth praises her.

beats.scene: Anne sits very still with her hand over her eyes behind the hedge
beats.summary: Anne feels the words were meant for her, because she let herself be persuaded long ago.

beats.scene: Mary sits on a stile, pouting, while Charles looks at her helplessly
beats.summary: Mary tires on the walk and sulks, and Anne is left alone with her thoughts.

beats.scene: Admiral Croft drives a small open carriage toward them along the lane
beats.summary: The Crofts come by in their small carriage, and Mrs Croft offers Anne a lift.

beats.scene: Mrs Croft takes the reins calmly as the little carriage tips toward a ditch
beats.summary: The Admiral nearly overturns the carriage, and Mrs Croft takes the reins calmly.

beats.scene: The Admiral speaks cheerfully to Anne as they drive along
beats.summary: The Admiral says that Wentworth will soon marry one of the Miss Musgroves, and Anne listens quietly.

beats.scene: Wentworth points at a map of the coast while the Musgrove sisters watch
beats.summary: Wentworth speaks of his friend Captain Harville at Lyme, and the sisters beg to see the sea.

beats.scene: A carriage stands in the early morning light with the party climbing in
beats.summary: The party sets off for Lyme in November: Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa and Wentworth.

beats.scene: The bay of Lyme shines blue below a steep street of old houses
beats.summary: They come down a steep hill into Lyme, and the bay lies shining below them.

beats.scene: The party walks along the stone quay of Lyme beside the grey sea
beats.summary: The party takes rooms at an inn and walks along the Cobb, the great stone wall of the harbour.

beats.scene: Captain Harville greets the visitors in a very small crowded house
beats.summary: They meet Captain Harville, a lame naval friend, at his small house near the harbour.

beats.scene: Captain Harville shows a shelf he made while his children play nearby
beats.summary: The Harvilles' tiny rooms are full of clever things Captain Harville has made himself.

beats.scene: Everyone crowds around a table as Mrs Harville serves a warm dinner
beats.summary: The Harvilles insist on feeding everyone, and Anne is moved by their warmth and loyalty to each other.

beats.scene: Captain Benwick sits apart in a black coat with a book in his hand
beats.summary: A quiet naval officer, Captain Benwick, is introduced, and his fiancee Fanny Harville has died.

beats.scene: Benwick and Anne walk together on the beach and talk of poetry
beats.summary: Benwick talks to Anne about poetry on the beach, and his words are full of sorrow.

beats.scene: Anne speaks gently to Benwick as the waves break on the shore
beats.summary: Anne gently advises Benwick to read less poetry and more cheerful, useful books.

beats.scene: Anne and the Musgrove sisters walk on the sand in the morning light
beats.summary: The next morning Anne and the Musgrove sisters go early to look at the sea.

beats.scene: A stranger on a Lyme beach looks admiringly at Anne as Wentworth watches
beats.summary: A stranger passing on the beach looks at Anne with open admiration, and Wentworth notices it.

beats.scene: Wentworth turns his head to look at Anne after the stranger passes
beats.summary: Wentworth gives Anne a look that tells her she is pretty again, and she is confused.

beats.scene: A gentleman steps from the inn into a waiting carriage with a servant
beats.summary: Back at the inn, the stranger is seen again, getting into his carriage, in mourning dress.

beats.scene: Louisa stands on the high steps of the Cobb with her arms outstretched
beats.summary: Walking on the Cobb, Louisa insists on jumping down the steps into Wentworth's arms.

beats.scene: Wentworth shakes his head at Louisa on the steps of the Cobb
beats.summary: Louisa wants to jump again from the higher steps, and Wentworth warns her that the pavement is hard.

beats.scene: Louisa leaps from the top steps of the Cobb with her arms stretched out
beats.summary: Louisa leaps before Wentworth is ready, and he cannot catch her in time.

beats.scene: Wentworth kneels by the pale unconscious Louisa on the stone wall
beats.summary: Louisa lies still as if dead, and Wentworth cries out in despair.

beats.scene: Mary shrieks and Henrietta faints while Charles stares in confusion
beats.summary: Mary screams, Henrietta faints, and Charles is helpless, so nobody knows what to do.

beats.scene: Anne points at Charles and Wentworth and gives clear orders
beats.summary: Anne alone keeps calm, tells Charles to help, and sends Benwick to fetch a surgeon.

beats.scene: A crowd gathers on the Cobb as Captain Harville bends over Louisa
beats.summary: A crowd gathers on the Cobb, and Captain Harville arrives and helps to lift Louisa.

beats.scene: Men carry Louisa on a plank through a narrow Lyme street
beats.summary: Louisa is carried to the Harvilles' house, and Anne holds the weeping Henrietta on the way.

beats.scene: A surgeon examines Louisa in a small bedroom while others wait
beats.summary: The surgeon says Louisa has hurt her head badly, but he hopes she will live.

beats.scene: Mrs Harville sets a pillow beneath Louisa's head in her own bed
beats.summary: Mrs Harville and her kind nurse offer to care for Louisa in their own tiny house.

beats.scene: Mary sits crying in a chair while Anne stands quietly beside her
beats.summary: Mary insists on staying to nurse Louisa, and Anne is told to go home instead.

beats.scene: Wentworth and Anne speak quietly at a window in the dim light
beats.summary: Wentworth tells Anne that she must be the one to break the news at Uppercross.

beats.scene: Wentworth helps Anne into a chaise at dusk before the long drive
beats.summary: Wentworth hires a carriage himself and helps Anne in, with one long look.

beats.scene: A carriage drives slowly through a dark road with two silent women inside
beats.summary: Anne, Charles and Henrietta drive home in the dark, and Henrietta weeps all the way.

beats.scene: Mrs Musgrove hurries a bundle into a coach at the Great House door
beats.summary: Mr and Mrs Musgrove hear the news with grief, and Mrs Musgrove sets out for Lyme at once.

beats.scene: Lady Russell greets Anne with a warm embrace at the cottage door
beats.summary: Lady Russell comes to Uppercross, and Anne leaves with her for Bath while Louisa heals at Lyme.

beats.scene: Lady Russell and Anne sit in a carriage with a pleasant winter view
beats.summary: Lady Russell notices that Anne looks better, and she credits the sea air.

beats.scene: Rooftops and chimneys of Bath rise in rain and smoke
beats.summary: They come to Bath in rain and smoke, and Anne would rather be in the country.

beats.scene: Lady Russell looks over a neat drawing room in a rented house
beats.summary: Lady Russell settles in a comfortable house in Rivers Street, not far from the Elliots.

beats.scene: Sir Walter and Elizabeth show off their rented house in Bath
beats.summary: In Bath, Sir Walter and Elizabeth live in grand rooms in Camden Place, and they show them off proudly.

beats.scene: Elizabeth smiles coldly while talking of fashionable visitors in the drawing room
beats.summary: Elizabeth speaks of grand visitors and fine parties, and nobody asks Anne about Lyme.

beats.scene: Mrs Clay smiles sweetly at Sir Walter and offers him a cup of tea
beats.summary: Mrs Clay is still living with the Elliots, and she is always pleasant and attentive to Sir Walter.

beats.scene: Sir Walter looks disapprovingly at passers-by from a drawing-room window
beats.summary: Sir Walter complains that Bath is full of plain faces and counts ugly women in one street.

beats.scene: Elizabeth reads a visiting card with great respect in the drawing room
beats.summary: Sir Walter and Elizabeth are eager to know their grand cousin Lady Dalrymple.

beats.scene: Sir Walter speaks of his cousin and heir while pointing to a family tree
beats.summary: Sir Walter tells Anne about their cousin Mr William Elliot, who will inherit the title but has been distant.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot, a courteous gentleman, bows to Sir Walter in the drawing room
beats.summary: Mr William Elliot calls at Camden Place, makes peace with the family and charms everyone.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot talks with a smile in the drawing room while the family listens
beats.summary: Mr Elliot explains his long silence, and he talks with such good sense that Sir Walter is charmed.

beats.scene: Anne looks closely at Mr Elliot's face and remembers a stranger
beats.summary: Anne realises that Mr Elliot is the same gentleman who admired her on the beach at Lyme.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot bows gracefully to Anne while she blushes
beats.summary: Mr Elliot confesses that he saw her at Lyme and is glad to be able to know her.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot sits by Anne at the Camden Place dinner table
beats.summary: Mr Elliot dines with the family and talks to Anne with great attention and good sense.

beats.scene: Lady Russell smiles warmly as she is introduced to Mr Elliot
beats.summary: Lady Russell meets Mr Elliot and is delighted, because he is polite, rational and rich.

beats.scene: Lady Russell takes Anne's hand and speaks kindly beside the fire
beats.summary: Lady Russell hopes Anne will marry Mr Elliot and become mistress of Kellynch like her mother.

beats.scene: Anne sits thoughtfully at a window and studies the street below
beats.summary: Anne wonders why Mr Elliot is so perfect, and she cannot quite trust a man who is never angry.

beats.scene: An old teacher speaks to Anne in a shop doorway in Bath
beats.summary: Anne hears from an old teacher that her school friend, now Mrs Smith, is lodging in Bath.

beats.scene: Anne climbs the stairs of a poor Bath house to visit a sick lady
beats.summary: Anne finds Mrs Smith in two small rooms in Westgate Buildings and is shocked at her condition.

beats.scene: Mrs Smith smiles from a chair beside her nurse, Mrs Rooke
beats.summary: Mrs Smith is cheerful in spite of her troubles, and her nurse Mrs Rooke helps her.

beats.scene: Elizabeth lifts her chin in horror at the sound of a poor street name
beats.summary: Anne mentions Mrs Smith, and Elizabeth is horrified that she visits Westgate Buildings.

beats.scene: Anne declines an invitation while Elizabeth stares at her in disbelief
beats.summary: Anne chooses to visit Mrs Smith rather than go to a fashionable evening party.

beats.scene: Mrs Smith shows Anne small knitted things she has made and sells
beats.summary: Mrs Smith earns a little by making small things, and she talks with humour of her narrow life.

beats.scene: Anne reads a letter from Mary at a table in Rivers Street
beats.summary: A letter from Mary says that Louisa is slowly getting better at Lyme.

beats.scene: Captain Benwick reads aloud beside Louisa's sofa in a small room
beats.summary: Mary writes that Captain Benwick is always beside Louisa, reading to her.

beats.scene: Admiral Croft and Mrs Croft step out of a carriage in a Bath street
beats.summary: The Crofts arrive in Bath because the Admiral's gout needs the waters.

beats.scene: The Admiral laughs while Anne listens with wide eyes in a drawing room
beats.summary: The Admiral tells Anne that Louisa Musgrove is to marry Captain Benwick, not Wentworth.

beats.scene: Anne sits very still, with colour rising in her cheeks
beats.summary: Anne realises that Wentworth is free, and she hides her feelings.

beats.scene: Mrs Croft speaks gently to Anne in a quiet corner of the room
beats.summary: Mrs Croft says her brother behaved well and will be glad to be clear of the mistake.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot bows farewell to Anne at the door of Camden Place
beats.summary: Mr Elliot tells Anne that he must leave Bath for a day or two and seems unwilling to go.

beats.scene: Captain Wentworth appears in a crowded Bath street as Anne turns
beats.summary: Anne is walking in Milsom Street in the rain when she suddenly sees Wentworth.

beats.scene: Wentworth bows awkwardly to Anne under a shop awning in the rain
beats.summary: Wentworth speaks to Anne with some embarrassment and asks after her friends.

beats.scene: Lady Russell looks from her carriage at a tall naval officer
beats.summary: Lady Russell sees Wentworth from her carriage and cannot help looking at him closely.

beats.scene: A party arrives at the White Hart inn with bags and bandboxes
beats.summary: Mrs Musgrove, Mary, Charles, Henrietta and Mr Hayter arrive in Bath and take rooms at the White Hart.

beats.scene: Henrietta laughs happily beside Charles Hayter in the parlour at the inn
beats.summary: Anne finds Henrietta happily engaged to Charles Hayter, since Wentworth is out of her thoughts.

beats.scene: Wentworth watches from across the street as Anne walks beside Mr Elliot
beats.summary: Wentworth sees Anne walking with Mr Elliot and believes they are close.

beats.scene: Mary lowers her voice and leans toward Anne at the White Hart
beats.summary: Mary tells Anne that the town believes she will marry Mr Elliot, and that Wentworth has heard it.

beats.scene: Anne lies awake in a dark room with her eyes open
beats.summary: Anne cannot sleep, because she cannot explain herself to Wentworth.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot offers Anne his arm at the door of Camden Place
beats.summary: Mr Elliot asks to escort Anne to the concert, and she cannot refuse him politely.

beats.scene: Mrs Smith watches Anne closely from her chair in the little room
beats.summary: Mrs Smith notices Anne's glow and asks whether she is going to marry Mr Elliot.

beats.scene: Mrs Smith speaks earnestly to Anne from her chair by the fire
beats.summary: Mrs Smith tells Anne that Mr Elliot is cold and selfish and has no heart.

beats.scene: Two young men laugh together in a London room long ago
beats.summary: Mrs Smith explains that long ago Mr Elliot was a friend of her husband and their frequent guest.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot laughs carelessly at a gentleman's table
beats.summary: In those days Mr Elliot spoke lightly of his family and cared nothing for honour, only money.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot stands beside a rich young woman at a church altar
beats.summary: Mr Elliot married a rich woman of low birth for her money, and he dropped the Smiths soon after.

beats.scene: Mr Smith lies ill in a dim room as his wife sits beside him
beats.summary: Mr Smith lost his fortune and his health, and he died, leaving his wife poor and ill.

beats.scene: A lawyer's letter lies unanswered on a desk
beats.summary: Mr Smith named Mr Elliot to settle his affairs, but Mr Elliot refused to act.

beats.scene: A ship sails away across the sea toward distant islands
beats.summary: Mrs Smith says her husband owned property in the West Indies, which Mr Elliot could have helped her to claim.

beats.scene: Mrs Rooke whispers a secret to Mrs Smith in the doorway
beats.summary: Mrs Smith's nurse, Mrs Rooke, has learned Mr Elliot's plans from one of her other patients.

beats.scene: Mrs Clay whispers to Sir Walter while Mr Elliot watches closely
beats.summary: Mr Elliot courts Anne to stay close to Sir Walter and keep Mrs Clay from becoming Lady Elliot.

beats.scene: Anne walks slowly home through the busy streets, deep in thought
beats.summary: Anne is shocked, thanks Mrs Smith and promises to help her recover her husband's property.

beats.scene: Anne in an evening dress looks at Mr Elliot across a candlelit room
beats.summary: Anne sees Mr Elliot with new eyes at Camden Place, but she keeps her face calm.

beats.scene: A line of sedan chairs carries ladies to the Octagon Room at night
beats.summary: The whole party travels to the grand concert in the Octagon Room.

beats.scene: Elegant guests crowd the Octagon Room at a concert in Bath
beats.summary: In the crowded room Sir Walter and Elizabeth look for Lady Dalrymple, and Anne looks for Wentworth.

beats.scene: Wentworth walks into the concert room with the Musgrove party
beats.summary: Wentworth arrives late with a party of friends and sits near Anne at last.

beats.scene: Wentworth speaks to Anne about Benwick near a pillar
beats.summary: Wentworth and Anne speak of Benwick and Louisa, and the talk is almost friendly.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot hands Anne a programme and points at a line of Italian
beats.summary: Mr Elliot asks Anne to translate an Italian song and draws her away from Wentworth.

beats.scene: Mr Elliot leans close to Anne while Wentworth stands stiffly nearby
beats.summary: Mr Elliot speaks softly to Anne, and Wentworth, jealous, stands stiff and silent.

beats.scene: Wentworth bows coldly to Anne and turns away through the crowd
beats.summary: Wentworth says a cold goodbye and walks out before the music is over.

beats.scene: Anne sits with her hands folded as the singers perform
beats.summary: Anne sits through the rest of the concert with a heavy heart, and hears nothing.

B1B2: Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall was a vain man who loved his own face and his own name. Every evening he opened the book of noble families and read the page that told his story.
Lady Elliot had died fourteen years before, and Sir Walter had never married again. He lived at Kellynch Hall with his three daughters, and he was proud of them for different reasons.
Elizabeth was sixteen when her mother died, and she had been mistress of the house ever since. She was handsome and clever, but she had her father's pride and very little of her mother's kindness.
Anne was gentle, clever and kind, and she was only twenty-seven, but her bloom was gone. Her father and her sister thought nothing of her opinion, however good it was.
Mary, the youngest, had married Charles Musgrove, the son of a rich family at Uppercross. She lived only three miles away, and she was always sure that she was ill.
Lady Russell was a widow who lived at Kellynch Lodge, and she had been the best friend of Anne's mother. She was the only person who truly valued Anne, and Anne trusted her more than anyone.
Sir Walter loved fine clothes, grand dinners and handsome furniture, and he had spent far more than he earned. His debts grew every year, and nobody dared to tell him how large they had become.
Mr Shepherd was Sir Walter's lawyer, a smooth and careful man who disliked unwelcome news. He knew exactly how much was owed, but he waited for Lady Russell to speak of the trouble first.
Lady Russell drew up a careful plan to cut the family's spending and pay off the debts. Sir Walter read it with horror, because it asked him to give up almost every comfort he loved.

At last Mr Shepherd suggested that the family should rent Kellynch Hall and live more cheaply in Bath. Sir Walter hated the thought of strangers in his house, but he disliked the thought of paying bills even more.
Mr Shepherd told Sir Walter that a very rich naval officer was looking for a house in Somerset. The war was ending, and many sailors were coming home with large fortunes.
Sir Walter said that the navy gave men of low birth too much honour and too much power. He also said it was a terrible profession for the face, because sun and wind made every sailor look old.
Sir Walter once met Admiral Baldwin, and he never forgot the sight of that brown, wrinkled face. He said that he had taken the man for sixty, when he was really only forty.
Mr Shepherd answered that a naval tenant would pay his rent on time and look after the house very carefully. He added that an admiral would feel honoured to live in the home of a baronet.
Mr Shepherd then said that the admiral's wife had a brother who once lived in the neighbourhood. This brother, a Mr Wentworth, had been the curate at Monkford some years before.
Sir Walter did not remember any Wentworth at all, and he said that the name meant nothing to him. Anne turned her face to the window, because she knew it far too well.

That evening Anne walked alone in the grounds of Kellynch, and her thoughts went back eight years. She had been nineteen then, and a young man called Frederick Wentworth had come to the village for the summer.
Frederick Wentworth was a clever, lively young man, full of wit and confidence, and he had no fortune at all. In a few weeks he and Anne were deeply in love, and they were soon engaged.
When Sir Walter heard about the engagement, he was cold and furious. He said that a poor sailor with no family was not good enough for an Elliot, and he refused all help.
Lady Russell loved Anne, and she was afraid that the young man would never be able to support a wife. She talked to Anne for many days, and at last Anne gave way and ended the engagement.
Wentworth sailed away with his heart full of anger, and Anne watched the empty sea for many days. She told no one how much she suffered, because she did not want to seem weak.
Wentworth was clever and lucky, and he rose quickly in the navy. He took several enemy ships in the war, and each one made him richer and more famous.
In eight years Anne's youth and bloom had slowly gone, and her father often said that she looked thin and haggard. Nobody thought of her as a pretty woman any more, and she did not argue with them.

When Anne was twenty-two, Charles Musgrove had asked her to marry him, and he was a good man from a good family. She had said no, because she could not love anyone but Wentworth, and Charles soon married her sister Mary.

Anne never blamed Lady Russell for the advice she had given, because it had come from love. She believed she had been right to listen to an older friend, although she would not have advised another girl to do the same.
Admiral Croft came to see Kellynch Hall, and he was a cheerful, honest man with a brown face. Sir Walter had expected a rough sailor, and he was surprised to find the man quite polite.
In Sir Walter's dressing room the Admiral found so many mirrors that he laughed out loud. He said that a man could not move without meeting himself, and Sir Walter agreed to take most of them away.

Mrs Croft was a short, brown, direct woman, and she told Anne that she had sailed with her husband for years. When she spoke of her brother Frederick, Anne understood that this was the very Captain Wentworth she had known.
The terms were soon agreed, and the Admiral promised to take good care of the house and the gardens. Sir Walter signed the paper with a grand air, as if he were doing the Admiral a favour.
When the day came, Sir Walter, Elizabeth and Mrs Clay left Kellynch for Bath in the family carriage. Anne stood on the steps and waved, and she felt more sadness at leaving the house than they did.
In September Anne went to stay with her sister Mary at Uppercross, only three miles away. The cottage was small and old, and it stood beside the large house of the Musgrove family.
Mary was lying on the sofa when Anne came in, and she said that she had been ill all week. She also said that nobody cared about her, and that Charles had gone out shooting again.
Mary had two small sons, Charles and Walter, and they were loud, quick and badly behaved. Mary could not control them, and she told Anne that they gave her a terrible headache.
Mr and Mrs Musgrove lived in the Great House, and they were old-fashioned, simple and very kind. Their house was always full of visitors, and there was always a fire and a place at the table.
The Musgroves had two pretty daughters, Louisa and Henrietta, who were nineteen and twenty. They were cheerful girls who liked dancing and music, and they had learned very little else.
Henrietta was fond of her cousin Charles Hayter, a young clergyman who lived nearby. Mary thought the Hayters were not good enough for the Musgroves, but Henrietta did not agree with her.
Anne was fond of music, and in the evenings she played the piano for the young people to dance. Nobody asked her to dance, and she did not mind, because she liked to watch them enjoy themselves.

Mary and Mrs Musgrove often quarrelled over small things, such as servants and children and who had said what. Anne listened to both of them, made them both feel better, and was useful to everyone in the house.
One evening Mrs Musgrove spoke of her son Dick, who had died at sea some years before. He had been a troublesome and idle boy, but now that he was dead, his mother remembered him with great love.
One morning Charles came home with news from Kellynch. Admiral Croft had said that his wife's brother, Captain Wentworth, would soon arrive to stay with them, and Anne felt her heart leap.
That night Anne sat alone with her sewing in her lap and could not make a single stitch. She was going to meet Wentworth again, and she did not know what she would feel.

Anne reasoned with herself quietly all through the long, sleepless night. Eight years had changed everything, she thought, and a man so full of success must have forgotten a girl he once knew for a summer.
Charles rode to Kellynch to meet Captain Wentworth, and he came home delighted with him. He had asked the Captain to visit Uppercross the very next morning, and Mary was very excited.
The next morning Anne was sitting with Mary when she heard a man's voice at the door. She knew it at once, although she had not heard it for eight years.
Wentworth came into the room with Charles, and he bowed to Anne with perfect politeness. He said a few words about the weather and then turned away, as if she were any ordinary acquaintance.
Wentworth sat with Mary and Charles for half an hour, and he talked and laughed with great ease. To Anne he said almost nothing, and when their eyes met by chance, he looked away at once.
When Wentworth left, Anne heard him speaking to Henrietta in the next room. He said that she was so much altered that he would hardly have known her.
The words hurt Anne deeply, but she told herself that they were true. She had been thin and pale for eight years, and she knew that much of the pain behind it had been his.
That evening the whole party dined at the Great House, and Wentworth sat between the two Musgrove sisters. He laughed with them and told them stories, and he asked Anne nothing at all.
Anne walked home alone along the dark lane, and she told herself that Wentworth meant nothing to her now. It was a brave speech, but she did not believe a single word of it.
After that first day Wentworth came to Uppercross almost every morning. Before long the Musgroves treated him like a son, and his chair at the Great House was always ready.
At dinner Wentworth told long, exciting stories about his ships and the battles he had seen. Everyone leaned forward to listen, and Anne listened too, although she kept her eyes on her plate.
Mrs Musgrove told Wentworth that her son Dick had once served under him on his ship. Wentworth had known Dick as a poor sailor, but he spoke kindly to the sad mother.
One evening Wentworth said that he wanted a wife with a firm mind and a sweet manner. The Musgrove sisters looked at him eagerly, and neither of them looked at Anne.
Anne played for the dancing that evening, and Wentworth danced with Louisa and then with Henrietta. When the music stopped, he thanked her with a short, cool bow and said no more.
Charles Hayter came back from his work and hoped for a warm welcome from Henrietta. She was so interested in Wentworth that she hardly noticed him, and poor Hayter went away unhappy.
Mary's elder son fell from a tree and badly hurt his collarbone. The doctor came at once and put it right, but the child was in pain and everyone in the cottage was frightened.
That evening Charles went to dinner at the Great House, because the doctor said the boy would be well. Mary was angry that he left her, but Anne stayed with the child and nursed him.
The next day Wentworth came to the cottage, and little Walter climbed onto Anne's back. She tried to move him gently, but the boy held on tightly and would not get down.
Without a word Wentworth stepped forward and lifted the boy from her back. Anne could not find her voice to thank him, and he left the room before she could speak.
On a bright autumn morning the young people planned a long walk to Winthrop, and Anne agreed to join them. Mary came too, although she said that she would be too tired to reach the end.
Anne walked slowly behind the party and enjoyed the autumn. The leaves were yellow, the fields were brown, and she found a small comfort in the quiet beauty of the season.
The party stopped beside a hedge heavy with nuts, and everyone began to pick them. Anne, who was tired, sat down on a bank behind the hedge and rested.
Anne heard Wentworth speaking to Louisa on the other side of the hedge. He held up a smooth nut and said that a firm mind was like a nut that had not fallen from the tree.
Louisa said that she would never let anyone persuade her against what she believed was right. Wentworth praised her warmly, and he said that this was exactly the quality he admired.
Anne felt that the words had been spoken for her ears, and that Wentworth wished her to know what he thought of her. She had allowed herself to be persuaded, and he had never forgiven it.
Mary sat down on a stile and said she was tired of walking and would go no farther. Charles tried to cheer her, but Anne was so lost in thought that she hardly heard them.
The Crofts came along the lane in their small open carriage, and Mrs Croft saw that Anne looked tired. She offered Anne a ride home, and Anne gladly accepted.
The Admiral drove badly, and the little carriage almost tipped over into the ditch twice. Mrs Croft quietly took the reins from his hand and made the horse go straight.
As they drove, the Admiral said that his brother-in-law was surely in love with one of the Miss Musgroves. He did not know which one, but he was sure that a wedding was coming.
One evening Wentworth spoke warmly about his friend Captain Harville, who lived by the sea at Lyme. The Musgrove sisters had never seen the sea in winter, and they begged to go at once.
The party left in the cold dawn of a November morning: Charles and Mary, Anne, the two sisters and Wentworth. Mary complained about the cold, but everyone else was in the highest spirits.
After many hours they came down a steep hill into the old town of Lyme, and the bay lay blue below them. Even Mary stopped complaining for a moment, because the view was so lovely.
The party took rooms at a small inn near the sea, and then went to look at the town. They walked as far as the Cobb, the long stone wall that curves around the harbour of Lyme.
Wentworth led them to Captain Harville's house, which stood in a narrow street near the harbour. It was tiny, but the Captain welcomed them as warmly as if it had been a palace.
Captain Harville had made shelves, tables and little cupboards with his own hands, and he showed them to the guests with pride. He said that sailors learn to make good use of small spaces.

The Harvilles insisted that the whole party stay for dinner, though there was hardly room to seat them. Mrs Harville was warm and gentle, and Anne was touched by the kindness of the sailors toward one another.
In the corner sat a young naval officer, Captain Benwick, dressed all in black. He had been engaged to Captain Harville's sister Fanny, who had died only a few months before.
After dinner Benwick walked with Anne along the beach and began to talk about poetry. He knew many poems by heart, and he quoted the saddest ones in a low, trembling voice.

Anne gently suggested that he should read less poetry and more good prose, and she named a few books that might help him. He thanked her sincerely, and said that nobody had spoken so kindly to him for months.
Early the next morning Anne and the two Musgrove sisters went down to the beach to see the sea. The sky was bright, the air was fresh, and a little colour had come back into Anne's pale face.
A gentleman passed them on the beach, and he looked at Anne with open admiration. Wentworth, who was walking close behind, noticed the look, and he glanced at her too.
Wentworth gave Anne a quick look that seemed to say he had noticed her bloom at last. She was so confused by it that she did not know where to look.
Back at the inn Anne saw the same gentleman again, getting into a carriage with his servant. She noticed that he was dressed in mourning, and he bowed politely as the carriage drove away.
On the Cobb the party walked along the high wall. Louisa insisted on jumping down the steps, and Wentworth caught her gently and set her on her feet.
Louisa laughed and wanted to jump again, this time from the higher steps. Wentworth told her that the pavement was hard and the jump was too high, but she would not listen.
Louisa leaped from the high steps before Wentworth was ready for her. He reached out to catch her, but his hands closed on empty air, and she fell to the stones.
Louisa lay perfectly still on the stones, with her eyes closed and her face as pale as chalk. Wentworth knelt beside her, and in horror he cried that she was dead.
Mary screamed loudly and Henrietta fainted, falling against Anne's arm. Charles stared at Louisa with a pale face, and nobody seemed to know what to do.
Anne alone kept her head in the crisis, and her voice was steady. She told Charles to help Wentworth, and she asked Captain Benwick, who had just arrived, to run for a surgeon at once.
Soon a crowd of curious people had gathered around them on the Cobb. Captain Harville arrived, and he helped Wentworth lift the girl, who still had not opened her eyes.
Four men carried Louisa on a plank through the narrow streets of Lyme to Captain Harville's house. Anne walked behind, holding Henrietta's arm, and the whole sad party followed in silence.
The surgeon examined Louisa for a long time, and then he said that she had hurt her head very badly. He did not think she would die, but she would need many weeks of quiet rest.
Mrs Harville said that Louisa must stay in her own house, where she and a kind nurse would look after her. The house was crowded, but nobody in it complained about it for a moment.
Mary insisted that she should stay and nurse Louisa, and that Anne must go home instead. Anne was ready to stay, but she saw that arguing with Mary would only make the trouble worse.
Wentworth told Anne quietly that somebody must take the news to Mr and Mrs Musgrove, and that Anne must be the one. He said that nobody else could do it with so much calm and kindness.
Wentworth himself found a carriage for the journey, and he helped Anne into it with great care. He looked at her for a moment without speaking, and then he stepped back and closed the door.
The three of them drove back to Uppercross through the dark, and nobody spoke much. Henrietta wept quietly most of the way, and Anne held her hand and thought about the look on Wentworth's face.
Anne told Mr and Mrs Musgrove the news as gently as she could, and they were deeply shocked. Mrs Musgrove packed her bags and went to Lyme at once to be with her daughter.
A few weeks later Lady Russell arrived at Uppercross, and she embraced Anne warmly. Louisa was slowly getting better at Lyme, so Anne could leave with a quiet mind and go to Bath.
On the road to Bath Lady Russell looked at Anne carefully and said that she looked much better. She believed that the sea air at Lyme had brought back some of Anne's youth.
They reached Bath in a heavy rain, and the whole city seemed to be wrapped in smoke. Lady Russell was pleased to be in a place with so many friends, but Anne longed for the green fields of Somerset.
Lady Russell took a comfortable house in Rivers Street, which was not far from the home of the Elliots. She was glad to have Anne with her, and she hoped to see her happily married.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth were living in Camden Place, in a tall and grand house in a very good part of Bath. They were proud of it, and they showed Anne every room as if she had never seen a fine house before.
Elizabeth talked about the parties she had been to and the important people she had met in Bath. Nobody asked Anne about Uppercross or Lyme, and she soon grew tired of listening.
Mrs Clay was still living with the Elliots, and Anne noticed at once how sweetly she smiled at Sir Walter. She laughed at all his jokes and agreed with all his opinions, and Anne felt uneasy.
Sir Walter said that Bath was full of plain faces, and that he had counted more than fifty ugly women in a single street. He was sure that nobody else had such a handsome face as his own.
Sir Walter and Elizabeth were very anxious to be known to their cousin, Lady Dalrymple, who was a viscountess. She was dull and rather stupid, but she had a title, and that was all they cared about.
Sir Walter spoke about his cousin and heir, Mr William Elliot, who would one day take his title. Mr Elliot had been cold to the family for years, and he had married a rich woman of low birth.
The next day Mr Elliot called at Camden Place, and he was so polite that Sir Walter forgave him at once. He bowed, he smiled, and he said all the right things in a soft, smooth voice.
Mr Elliot explained that he had been young and foolish, and that he now valued his family very much. He spoke so calmly and so sensibly that Sir Walter was completely charmed.
As Mr Elliot turned toward the light, Anne suddenly realised who he was. He was the gentleman who had looked at her so admiringly on the beach at Lyme, and who had later driven away from the inn.
Mr Elliot told Anne that he had been struck by her at Lyme, and he was happy to learn she was his cousin. Anne blushed, because his words were gentle and well chosen.
Mr Elliot dined at Camden Place several times in the following week, and each time he spoke to Anne with more attention. He praised her sense and her taste, and she began to enjoy his company.
Lady Russell met Mr Elliot soon afterward, and she liked him at once. He was polite, sensible and rich, and she thought that he was exactly the kind of man she wanted for Anne.
Lady Russell hoped that Anne would marry Mr Elliot, and so become Lady Elliot of Kellynch Hall. She did not say so openly, but she dropped a few gentle hints.
Anne found that Mr Elliot was agreeable, but she did not entirely trust him. He was always polite and never angry, and she wondered whether he ever said exactly what he thought.
One morning Anne met her old teacher, who told her that her school friend Miss Hamilton was in Bath. She was now Mrs Smith, and she was a widow, and she was very poor and very ill.
Anne found Mrs Smith in two small rooms in Westgate Buildings, a poor and crowded part of Bath. She was shocked to see how thin and ill her old friend had become.
Mrs Smith greeted Anne with a bright smile, and she did not complain about her poverty or her pain. Her kind nurse, Mrs Rooke, looked after her, and the two old friends talked for a long time.
Anne mentioned that she had been visiting an old school friend in Westgate Buildings. Elizabeth was horrified, and she said that no lady of their rank should go to such a place.
Not long afterward, the family had an invitation to an evening party at Camden Place. Anne chose to spend the evening with Mrs Smith instead, and Elizabeth could hardly believe it.
Mrs Smith showed Anne the small things that she made and sold to earn a little money. She laughed about her narrow life, and said that she had learned to find pleasure in very small things.
A letter came from Mary, and it was full of news. Louisa was sitting up now, and the doctor said that she would be well again in time, though she was still very weak.
Mary also wrote that Captain Benwick sat with Louisa for hours every day, reading aloud to her. She laughed that Louisa seemed to like it, and that nobody could tell how it would end.
Admiral and Mrs Croft came to Bath, because the Admiral had been troubled by gout. They took lodgings near Camden Place and called on Sir Walter's family at once.
In the drawing room the Admiral told Anne some astonishing news. Louisa Musgrove was going to marry Captain Benwick, and not Frederick Wentworth at all.
Anne understood at once that Wentworth was free, and she felt a great wave of joy and fear. She bent her head over her work so that nobody would see her face.
Mrs Croft said quietly that her brother had never really been engaged. He had behaved with honour toward Louisa, she said, but she thought that he would be glad to be free.
Mr Elliot told Anne that he had to leave Bath for two days on business. He seemed very sorry to go, and he said that he hoped she would not forget him.
Anne was walking in Milsom Street on a rainy morning when she suddenly saw Captain Wentworth. She had not known that he was in Bath, and for a moment she could not speak.
Wentworth bowed to her, and he spoke with a kind of awkward care. He asked how she had been, and he spoke of Louisa's engagement, and Anne said that she was very glad for her.
Lady Russell passed in her carriage and saw Anne talking to a tall man in a naval coat. She asked who he was, and when Anne said his name, she looked at him for a long time.
Mrs Musgrove arrived in Bath with Mary, Charles and Henrietta, and Charles Hayter came with them. They took rooms at the White Hart, a large inn, to buy clothes and enjoy the town.
At the White Hart Anne learned that Henrietta was now engaged to Charles Hayter, and the whole family was happy. Henrietta had quite forgotten Wentworth, and she looked brighter than ever.
A day later Mr Elliot walked beside Anne along a Bath street, and he spoke to her with a smile. Across the road Wentworth saw them together, and he thought that they looked very close.
Mary told Anne that everyone in Bath thought she was going to marry Mr Elliot. She said that Wentworth had heard the story too, and Anne's heart sank.
That night Anne lay awake for a long time. She could not go to Wentworth and explain herself, and she did not know how to make him understand.
Mr Elliot told Anne that there would be a concert at the Octagon Room, and he asked to take her there. Lady Russell encouraged her to go, and Anne could not refuse him politely.

When Anne visited Mrs Smith, her friend watched her face and asked a blunt question. She wanted to know whether Anne was going to marry Mr Elliot, because the gossip had reached even Westgate Buildings.
Mrs Smith hesitated, and then she told Anne the truth about Mr Elliot. She said that he was a cold, selfish man who thought of nothing but his own comfort.
Many years before, Mrs Smith said, Mr Elliot had been a close friend of her husband. He had often dined at their house, and her husband had always lent him money.
Mrs Smith said that in those days Mr Elliot spoke of his family and its honour with contempt. He cared nothing for the title, and everything for money.
Soon after that, Mr Elliot married a rich woman of low birth, simply because of her fortune. He soon stopped visiting the Smiths, because he had no further use for them.
Mr Smith soon lost much of his money, and he fell ill with a long and painful illness. When he died, he left his wife poor, sick and almost alone.
Before he died, Mr Smith had asked Mr Elliot to take charge of his affairs. Mr Elliot refused to do it, and he never answered the letters that Mrs Smith wrote to him.
Mrs Smith said that her husband had owned some property in the West Indies. She believed that she could claim it, but she needed a friend to help her, and Mr Elliot had refused.
Mrs Smith said that her nurse, Mrs Rooke, had heard about Mr Elliot's plans from another lady she looked after. This lady was a close friend of Mr Elliot, and she knew a great deal about him.
Mrs Smith explained that Mr Elliot was afraid that Mrs Clay would marry Sir Walter and have a son. That son would take the title from Mr Elliot, so he was working hard to prevent it.
Anne was shocked, and she thanked Mrs Smith for her honesty. She promised that she would help her to claim her husband's property, and she walked home deep in thought.
That evening Mr Elliot arrived at Camden Place in his best clothes, and Anne watched him with new eyes. She was polite, but she could no longer believe a single word he said.
The Elliots and Lady Russell travelled to the concert in the Octagon Room, which was the grand event of the Bath season. Candles lit the street, and the carriages stood in a long line.
The Octagon Room was crowded with elegant ladies and gentlemen. Sir Walter and Elizabeth went to find Lady Dalrymple, and Anne looked along every row for Wentworth.
At last Wentworth came into the room with a group of friends from the White Hart. When he saw Anne, he stopped for a moment, and then he came toward her through the crowd.
Wentworth and Anne talked about Captain Benwick and Louisa Musgrove, and he admitted that he had been surprised. For the first time in years, their conversation seemed almost friendly.
Then Mr Elliot arrived, and he asked Anne to translate the Italian words of a song on the programme. She did so politely, but she could feel Wentworth watching them both.
Mr Elliot bent his head toward Anne and spoke to her very softly, and he used her name as if it belonged to him. Wentworth stood stiffly a few steps away, and his face was growing dark.
Wentworth said that he must go, and his voice was cold and very polite. He bowed to Anne, turned away, and walked out of the room before the concert had ended.
Anne stayed in her seat for the rest of the evening, and she did not hear a note of the music. She felt that she had lost the one moment that might have changed everything.
On the drive home Anne made up her mind. She would go to the White Hart in the morning, and she would find some way to let Wentworth see the truth.
The next morning Anne walked quickly to the White Hart, and her heart was beating fast. She was afraid, but she had made up her mind, and she did not turn back.
In the sitting room at the inn, Mrs Musgrove welcomed Anne warmly and began to talk about wedding clothes. She spoke of ribbons, shops and prices for a long time, and Anne listened politely.
At the other end of the room Wentworth was sitting at a desk, and he was writing a letter. He bowed to Anne when she came in, but he did not look up again.
Captain Harville arrived in Bath that morning, and he came to the White Hart. He sat down by Anne at the window, and the two of them began to talk quietly.
Captain Harville showed her a small portrait of Captain Benwick that had been painted for his dead sister Fanny. He had been asked to have it set in a new frame for Louisa Musgrove.
Captain Harville said sadly that his sister would not have forgotten Benwick so soon. He believed that men were more faithful than women, and that women forgot their loves sooner.
Anne answered that she would not accept the songs and stories as proof. The men had written them, she said, and men had always had every advantage in telling the tale.
Anne said quietly that the privilege of her sex was to love longest, even when hope was gone. She said that women could not help it, and she spoke as one who knew.

Captain Harville said that sailors felt deeply too, and he described a man leaving his wife and children for a long voyage at sea. Anne said that she did not doubt it, and that she only spoke of long loyalty.
Behind them there was a sudden noise as Wentworth dropped his pen on the floor. He had heard every word, and he rose and hurried out of the room without speaking.
Anne sat quite still with her heart racing, and the room seemed to go very quiet. Mrs Musgrove went on talking about ribbons, and Anne could not hear a word of it.
A few minutes later Wentworth came back into the room, saying that he had forgotten his gloves. He looked at Anne for a moment, and then he hurried out again.
Captain Harville went to the desk and saw a folded letter lying on the paper. It was addressed to Miss A E, and he handed it to her with a knowing smile.
Anne opened the letter with shaking hands and read it slowly. Wentworth wrote that he could no longer be silent, because what he had heard her say had touched him to the heart.
In the letter Wentworth said that he had never loved anyone but her. He admitted that he had been proud and unjust, but he said that he had never once been unfaithful to her.
Anne could not hold back her tears, and she rose to leave. Mrs Musgrove thought that she was unwell, and she kindly offered to send for a carriage.
Charles Musgrove offered to walk with Anne as far as Camden Place, because he had some business in the town. He talked cheerfully about his dogs, and Anne scarcely listened.
In the street they met Wentworth, who had been waiting and walking up and down. Charles said that he had an errand to do, and he gave Anne into Wentworth's care.
They walked together until they found a quiet gravel path where nobody else was walking. There Wentworth turned and spoke to her openly, as he had not spoken in eight years.
Wentworth told her that he had never stopped loving her, and that he had tried and failed to forget her. Anne answered that she had loved only him too, and her voice trembled with happiness.
Wentworth explained that he had never really loved Louisa Musgrove. He had been kind to her and her sisters, and then the accident had made it hard for him to step back.
Wentworth told Anne that on the Cobb he had seen how steady and strong she was. Louisa had been stubborn, he said, but Anne had a quiet strength that was worth far more.
Wentworth admitted that he had been angry for years, and that he had wanted to prove that he could do without her. He had been wrong, he said, and it had taken him a long time to understand it.

Anne told Wentworth that she had been right to follow Lady Russell's advice, although it had been very painful. She said that Lady Russell had stood in the place of a mother, and she had acted from duty.
Wentworth said that he had always blamed her advisers, but he now understood how a loving girl felt bound to obey them. He said that he should have been more patient.
Anne told Wentworth that she had never meant to marry Mr Elliot, and that she did not even trust him. Wentworth smiled, and he admitted that he had left the concert because he was so jealous.
The rain had stopped, and the sun was shining over the pale houses of Bath. For the first time Anne thought that the city was beautiful, and she was too happy to say so.
That evening Sir Walter held a party at Camden Place, and Wentworth came to it. Sir Walter was surprised to see how well-dressed and handsome the young man had become, and he was very polite.
Lady Russell watched Anne and Wentworth talk together across the room. She saw the joy in Anne's face and the care in Wentworth's, and she understood what had happened.
Mr Elliot, who stood near the door, saw Anne's face and understood that his hopes were gone. He bowed politely to everyone and left the party early.
The next day Wentworth asked Sir Walter for Anne's hand in marriage. He was now a rich and respected captain, and Sir Walter did not refuse him.
Lady Russell took Anne's hand and told her that she had been wrong about Wentworth eight years before. She admitted that she had misjudged him, and she asked Anne to forgive her.
Sir Walter took down his favourite book and wrote the news of Anne's marriage in it, with a flourish. He was quite content, because the name of Wentworth was now an honourable one.
Wentworth helped Mrs Smith to recover her husband's property in the West Indies, and she became comfortable at last. She was delighted to see her old friend so happy.
Soon afterward Mr Elliot left Bath, and it was discovered that Mrs Clay had gone with him. Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked, and they remembered that Anne had warned them.
When Mary heard the news, she was glad because Wentworth had money and a good name. She was a little jealous, too, and she said that Anne would have a grander house than hers.
Admiral and Mrs Croft were overjoyed to hear about the engagement. The Admiral laughed and shook Wentworth's hand until it hurt, and Mrs Croft kissed Anne warmly.
Anne and Wentworth were married in a quiet ceremony, with Lady Russell and their friends beside them. Anne wore a simple dress, and she had never felt so happy.
Anne was proud to be a sailor's wife, and she loved the Navy and its warm friendships. But she knew that if war came again, she would live in fear for him.
Anne and Wentworth stood together at the window and watched a ship sail far out on the grey sea. They had waited eight long years for this quiet moment, and it was worth every one of them.
C1C2: Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, in Somerset, kept one book beside his bed, and every morning he opened it at the page that held his own name. The volume listed the baronets of England, and the entry for his family recorded each birth, marriage and honour with a loving, solemn exactness. Nothing in it ever failed to soothe him, for vanity was the foundation of his character, and no page of it was ever dull.

Lady Elliot had been a sensible and affectionate woman, and her death, fourteen years earlier, had taken the only real check from her husband's folly. Sir Walter remained a widower, and nobody who knew him expected him to change his habits or his opinion of himself. His three daughters grew up in a house where rank was admired above every other virtue.

Elizabeth was only sixteen when she took her mother's place at the head of the table, and for fourteen years she had governed the household with great confidence and little warmth. She was tall, elegant and still handsome, and she believed, as her father did, that a good name and a fine face excused almost any fault. Her single regret was that no gentleman of the right rank had yet asked her to marry him.

Anne, the second daughter, had an elegance of mind and a sweetness of temper that her father and Elizabeth were quite unable to value. Her fine complexion had faded early, and her opinion, though it was always the wisest in the house, was rarely asked and never followed. She had learned to sit quietly in the corner of every room and to be useful to everyone there.

Mary, the youngest, had married a good-natured country gentleman named Charles Musgrove, whose family owned the great house at Uppercross, only three miles from Kellynch. Her husband was easy and kind, but Mary herself was of a restless and complaining temper, and she was never so happy as when she was describing her latest illness. She inherited her father's pride and her mother's anxiety, and she gained very little pleasure from either.

Lady Russell, a widow of good sense and strong principles, lived at Kellynch Lodge, and she had been the dearest friend of the late Lady Elliot. She had given her affection to the whole family, but it was Anne, with her sense and her sweetness, who held the largest share. In every difficulty of the household it was Lady Russell whom they consulted, and Anne in particular who never doubted her counsel.

Sir Walter was a man of expensive taste and an income that had never quite matched it, and year after year the difference had grown into a debt he could not ignore. He had been generous to his tradesmen, lavish to his friends and ruinously careful of his own appearance. Each new bill arrived like a small insult, and he laid the blame on everything and everybody except himself.

Mr Shepherd, the lawyer who managed Sir Walter's affairs, was a smooth, prudent man who preferred to let other people say the disagreeable thing. He knew to the last pound how deeply his client was in debt, and he had no wish to be the one who named the sum. Lady Russell, who had no such delicacy, finally persuaded him to help her bring the matter before Sir Walter.

Lady Russell, whose own affairs were in perfect order, drew up a careful plan of retrenchment, with every saving written out and every debt set against it. Sir Walter read it with a gathering sense of injury, since it demanded the loss of his carriage, his gifts and his extravagant dinners. He could not, he declared, give up a single thing that a gentleman of his rank was entitled to enjoy.

Mr Shepherd at last proposed the one remedy that a man of Sir Walter's feelings might consent to, which was to let Kellynch Hall to a suitable tenant and retire to a smaller house in Bath. The notion of strangers in his halls was painful, but the notion of living in a place where nobody knew his debts was a great deal less so. After a day of anguished consideration he agreed, and Anne, who had hoped for a quieter economy, was not asked for her opinion.

Mr Shepherd mentioned, with the air of a man introducing a pleasant surprise, that a naval officer of great fortune was seeking a house in that part of Somerset. The long war with France was drawing to its close, and the sea had made several fortunate men richer than the gentlemen on shore. Such a person, he suggested, would pay a handsome rent and ask very few questions.

Sir Walter declared that the navy was a very useful service but a very unfortunate one, since it lifted men of obscure birth into a distinction their grandfathers could never have imagined. It had a worse fault still, in his opinion, for the wind and the sun ruined the complexion and aged a man long before his time. A naval officer, in short, was a person who grew old and tanned at the country's expense.

Sir Walter then described a certain Admiral Baldwin, whom he had met in town, and whose deeply lined and weathered face had given him a lasting fright. He had taken the man for sixty years old at the least, and had been shocked to learn that the admiral was little more than forty. Nothing, Sir Walter said, could excuse a profession that did such things to a human face.

Mr Shepherd, who knew his client's weak points, replied that no tenant could be more suitable than a rich and careful officer, who would pay punctually and keep the gardens as neatly as a ship. He added, with a delicate bow, that any such person would be honoured to be the guest of so distinguished a family. Sir Walter found that this thought softened his opinion more than all the rent in England.

Mr Shepherd added, as a matter of small importance, that the admiral's wife had a brother who had once been the curate of Monkford, close to Kellynch. The name, he said, was Wentworth, and he supposed that Sir Walter would remember it well, since the young man had lived in the village for some time. He spoke the name lightly and could not have guessed what it did to the quiet woman at the window.

Sir Walter said that the name of Wentworth was perfectly unknown to him, and that curates were a class of persons he had never troubled to remember. Anne, who sat a little apart with a book open on her knee, felt her colour rise, and she turned her face to the window so that nobody should see it. It was not the curate who had made her blush, but the curate's brother.

That evening Anne walked alone beneath the old trees of Kellynch, and the name she had heard in the morning drew her thoughts back eight years. She had been nineteen in the summer of 1806, and a young naval officer named Frederick Wentworth had come to stay with his brother in the village. She had not known, as she watched him walk up the lane that first day, how entirely he would fill her life.

Frederick Wentworth was a brilliant young man, quick in his wit, ardent in his feelings and perfectly sure of his own future, though he possessed no fortune but his talent and his ship. Anne, who had never before been truly noticed by anyone, found his attention intoxicating, and within a few weeks the two had given each other their hearts. Never, in her whole life, had she been so happy as she was in those months.

Sir Walter received the news of the engagement with a silence that was worse than anger, and he declared at last that the match was a degrading one for his daughter. A penniless young man of no family, with nothing but his profession and his hopes, was not a person he could ever accept at his table. He would give nothing, he said, and he would say nothing, and he would certainly never help.

Lady Russell, who loved Anne as a daughter and distrusted a future built on hope alone, spoke to her seriously of the dangers of a long and uncertain engagement. She called it imprudent, improper and likely to bring Anne nothing but anxiety, and Anne, who trusted her friend more than herself, at last agreed to end it. Wentworth, hurt and proud, heard her decision in anger and left the neighbourhood and the country within a few days.

Wentworth went back to his ship in a state of angry pride, and Anne was left behind with a sorrow that no one in her family had noticed. She did her duty each day, ate her meals at the proper hour, and told nobody how much she suffered. Within a few weeks the cheerful girl of nineteen had become a quiet, thoughtful woman who looked at the sea and said very little.

Wentworth possessed the very qualities the navy rewarded: courage, quick judgement and a great deal of luck. He was soon promoted, he captured several enemy ships in the long war, and each prize filled his purse and enlarged his reputation. By the time the war was ending he was a captain with a handsome fortune and a name that was known in every port.

The years had taken the roses from her cheeks and the brightness from her eyes, and Sir Walter observed more than once that Anne had grown wonderfully thin and plain. Her bloom had been lost early, and with it, it seemed, her claim to the world's attention. She was only twenty-seven, but she had the manner of a woman who expected nothing more from life.

At the age of twenty-two Anne had received the only other offer of her life, from the amiable and respectable Charles Musgrove, who stood to inherit a fine estate. She had refused him gently, because her heart was still full of another, and Lady Russell, who had hoped for the match, was deeply disappointed. Charles had consoled himself within a year by marrying Mary, who was Anne's sister and nothing like her.

Anne never blamed Lady Russell, for the advice had been given in love and in the sincere belief that it served Anne's good. She held that she had been right to be guided by a trusted friend, and yet she knew, in the quiet of her own mind, that she would never urge another young woman to do as she had done. It is a hard thing to be right and to be unhappy for the whole of eight years.

Admiral Croft arrived to inspect Kellynch Hall, a broad, hearty, brown-faced man with the open manner of one who had spent his life among honest sailors. Sir Walter, who had prepared himself for a rude and wrinkled fellow, found the visitor so much better mannered than he had expected that he forgot to be disagreeable. The Admiral admired the house, praised the park, and said he had never seen a prettier place.

In Sir Walter's dressing room the Admiral stopped in astonishment, for the walls were crowded with large looking-glasses, each one polished to perfection. He declared, with a good-humoured laugh, that no sensible man could turn round in such a place without meeting himself coming the other way. Sir Walter, a little wounded but not displeased, consented that the mirrors should be moved before the new tenants moved in.

Mrs Croft was a short, weathered, direct woman of the kind who say what they mean and mean it kindly, and she told Anne cheerfully that she had sailed with her husband to the farthest corners of the world. In the course of their talk she spoke of her brother, Captain Frederick Wentworth, and the name fell upon Anne with the force of a bell. Anne answered calmly and walked a little farther along the path, but her hands had turned quite cold, and she did not trust herself to speak again.

The terms were soon agreed, the Admiral promised to keep the gardens as neatly as the deck of a ship, and Mr Shepherd produced the papers with a flourish. Sir Walter signed his name with all the dignity of a man conferring a gift, and neither party noticed that Anne stood motionless beside the door. The Hall, in which she had been born, now belonged to a stranger, and the stranger's wife was Wentworth's sister.

When the day of departure came, Sir Walter, Elizabeth and Mrs Clay climbed into the carriage with great ceremony and set off for Bath, a place where they were sure to be admired. Anne stood on the steps and waved until the wheels had vanished beyond the trees, and she felt more sorrow at the loss of the house than any of them. Then she turned and walked to Lady Russell's house, with her heart a little lighter, and her future entirely uncertain.

Anne's first visit after the family left was to Uppercross, where Mary lived in a small, old-fashioned cottage with a thatched roof and a crowded garden. The great house of the Musgroves stood only a short walk away, and everything about the neighbourhood spoke of country comfort and country habit. She expected to stay for a few weeks, and she had no idea how much would happen before she left.

Mary was stretched upon the sofa in a shabby room, and her first words to Anne were a complaint that she had been very ill indeed. Nobody had visited her, she said, her husband had gone out shooting without a thought for her, and she was quite certain that she would not live to see the winter. Anne, who had heard such speeches many times, listened kindly and went to ask the servant for tea.
