Mary's two young sons, Charles and Walter, were as boisterous as a pair of puppies, and they had been spoiled by an indulgent mother and a lenient father. Neither child paid the smallest attention to a command, and Mary, who could not manage them, complained that they gave her severe headaches. Anne found that the only way to keep the peace was to give each of them something to do.

Mr and Mrs Musgrove were warm-hearted, old-fashioned people who had never been interested in the new ideas of the great world. Their house had been furnished for comfort rather than for show, and the hearth was always burning and the table always laid for one more. Anne felt at once that she was welcome in a house where nobody thought it necessary to be clever.

Louisa and Henrietta, the two eldest daughters of the house, were young, pretty and overflowing with spirits, and they had been educated exactly as their neighbours' daughters were. They danced with energy, sang without shame and talked with enthusiasm about everything that had happened that week. Anne, who had been quiet from the age of nineteen, regarded their happiness with a mixture of pleasure and wistfulness.

Henrietta had formed a quiet attachment to her cousin Charles Hayter, a young clergyman of excellent character and rather uncertain prospects. Mary, who considered herself a daughter of baronets and therefore a person of rank, held that the Hayters were socially beneath the Musgroves, and she said so on every possible occasion. Henrietta, who loved him with a simple and steady heart, paid no attention whatever to her sister's opinion, and Charles Hayter remained her favourite visitor.

In the evenings Anne was often asked to play, since she had a good touch and a better temper than most of her companions, and the Musgrove girls could dance for hours while she sat at the instrument. Nobody ever thought to ask whether she might like to dance herself, and she had long since accepted that she was never to be thought of. She found a certain peace in playing for others, and she discovered that watching their happy faces was almost as satisfying as sharing in it herself.

Mary and Mrs Musgrove were forever offended by some trifle, whether it was a servant's insolence, a child's treatment or an invitation that had not been sent, and each came to Anne in turn with her injuries. Anne heard them both patiently, gave each a little sympathy and a great deal of common sense, and sent them away comforted. Within a fortnight she had made herself quite necessary to the whole neighbourhood, and quite unnoticed.

One evening Mrs Musgrove spoke at length of her eldest son, poor Dick, who had gone to sea as a very unpromising boy and had died there some years earlier. He had been stupid, wild and rather useless in his lifetime, but the passing years had wrapped him in a soft, golden remembrance, and she wept for him as for a hero. Anne, who knew the whole truth of the matter, said only what was kind, and she let the old woman cry without a word of correction.

One morning Charles came home with a piece of news that the whole neighbourhood would soon be discussing, which was that Captain Wentworth, the brother of Mrs Croft, was expected at Kellynch within the week. He mentioned the name lightly, as a man speaks of a coming holiday, and Mary clapped her hands in delight. Anne bent over her sewing and said nothing, but the needle trembled in her hand.

That night Anne sat alone with her sewing neglected in her lap, and she found that she could not make a single stitch. In a few days she would stand in a room with the man she had loved at nineteen, and she had no idea what her face or her voice would do. She told herself firmly that eight years had passed, and she took no comfort from the thought.

Anne reasoned with herself through the long hours of the night, as a sensible woman must. Time, she said, changes both feelings and faces, and a man whose life had been so full of action and success could scarcely give a passing thought to a girl he had known for a single summer. Having proved the point entirely to her own satisfaction, she lay awake until dawn.

Charles rode over to Kellynch the same afternoon to pay his respects, and he returned in the highest spirits, declaring that Captain Wentworth was the finest fellow he had ever met. He had invited him to Uppercross at once, and the Captain, who seemed not to dislike the idea, had promised to call the next morning. Mary spent the evening in raptures, and Anne spent it in a silence that nobody noticed.

The following morning Anne was sitting with Mary in the little parlour when she heard a man's step in the passage and a man's voice speaking to Charles. It was a voice she had not heard for eight years, and she recognised it at once, as one knows a melody that has never quite left the mind. The room seemed to grow very small, and she had barely time to compose her face.

Wentworth entered the parlour behind Charles, a little browner and a good deal firmer than the youth she remembered, and he bowed to her with a courtesy that was entirely without warmth. He addressed to her a few civil words about the weather and the journey and then turned to Mary, as though she were any other lady of his acquaintance. Anne curtsied and answered, and the whole affair was over in a minute, and she felt quite dizzy.

For half an hour Wentworth sat in the little parlour and talked with great animation to Mary and Charles, telling stories of his ships and his friends and his adventures on the sea. When he glanced toward Anne, which was seldom, his look was courteous, calm and perfectly empty, and she understood that she had become to him a person he must be polite to. It was the most painful thing she had ever endured, and she endured it without a word.

As Wentworth was leaving, Anne caught the sound of his voice in the passage, speaking to Henrietta, and she could not help hearing his words. He said that Miss Elliot was so altered that he should hardly have known her, and he said it without any anger at all, which was the worst of it. She stood quite still behind the half-open door until the footsteps had died away down the passage, and then she drew a long and unsteady breath.

The words struck her to the heart, though she reminded herself, with a kind of grim patience, that they were no more than the truth. Her bloom had gone, her youth had gone, and a great part of both had gone in grieving for him, a fact that he could not be expected to understand. She resolved that if he found her altered she would at least not be altered in manners.

The whole Uppercross party dined that evening at the Great House, and Wentworth, who had been placed between the two Musgrove sisters, seemed to find nothing to regret in his situation. He laughed, he teased, and he told tales of the sea in such a manner that the girls hung upon every word. Anne, seated across the table, watched him with great attention and received no sign of recognition whatever.

Anne walked back to the cottage by herself under the whispering autumn trees, and she told herself, in the firmest voice she could manage, that Captain Wentworth was now merely a gentleman of her acquaintance. It was a bold speech and a well-reasoned one, and she did not believe a word of it. Her heart, which she had thought entirely quiet after so many years of discipline, was beating as fast and as foolishly as a child's.

After that first day Wentworth became a regular visitor, riding over from Kellynch almost every morning, and he was soon received at the Great House like a favourite son. The Musgroves were delighted by his openness, his cheerful stories and his total absence of vanity. A place was kept for him at every table, and Anne, who watched all this from the corner, grew accustomed to the sound of his horse.

At dinner Wentworth told stories of his life at sea, of storms survived and prizes taken, of the ship he had loved best and the one he had very nearly lost. The Musgroves were enchanted, the young ladies asked a hundred questions, and even Mary forgot to complain. Anne kept her eyes upon her plate, and she heard every word, and she wished that her heart could be so careless as her face.

Mrs Musgrove, who had just made a discovery, told Captain Wentworth with tears in her eyes that her poor Dick had once served on his ship and had written of him very kindly. Wentworth, who remembered the young man as a stupid and troublesome sailor, listened with grave attention and spoke of him in the kindest terms. Anne saw his gentleness toward the foolish old woman, and it moved her more than she liked.

One evening, in the course of a lively conversation, Wentworth declared that he meant to marry soon, and that his wife must have a strong mind and a sweet manner. He would have no weak or yielding person, he said, and he looked about the room as he said it, and the two Musgrove sisters coloured with pleasure. Anne, who had been the weakest and most yielding of all, felt that the words were not meant for her.

The young people danced in the evening, and Anne played the piano for hours while Wentworth took the floor with one Musgrove sister after another. He never once asked her to dance, and when the music stopped at last, he thanked her with a short, cool bow that was the very model of good manners. She rose from the instrument with aching hands and a quiet, steady, unspoken grief.

Charles Hayter, who had been away for some weeks on his clerical business, came back to Uppercross in the hope of a warm welcome from his cousin Henrietta. He found her so charmed by the newly arrived Captain that she scarcely noticed him, and he went away with the look of a man who has been quietly insulted. Anne, who saw it all from her place in the corner, felt very sorry for both of them, and especially for the honest young man.

Mary's elder boy fell and injured his collarbone so severely that the whole household was thrown into confusion. The doctor was sent for, the bone was set, and the child was laid on the sofa with a very pale face, while his mother wept and wrung her hands. Anne, who was calm and quick, sat at the boy's side and did everything that needed doing.

That evening Charles, who had been assured by the doctor that all was well, put on his coat and went to the dinner at the Great House, to Mary's great indignation. She complained that her husband had no heart, she complained that she was left alone with a sick child, and she complained of her own head. Anne said nothing, sat down by the boy, and took his hot little hand in hers.

The next morning Wentworth called at the cottage to inquire after the invalid, and found Anne kneeling beside the sofa, with little Walter climbing upon her shoulders in spite of every gentle remonstrance. The child clung to her neck like a monkey and laughed at her efforts to dislodge him. Mary sat by and did nothing, and Anne grew hot and breathless and entirely unable to rise.

Without a word, Wentworth crossed the room, took the small tormentor firmly by the arms, and lifted him from Anne's back. He set the boy on the floor, said a few quiet words to him, and walked out of the cottage before she could speak. Anne sat for some time with her face hidden, overcome, not by the child's weight, but by the gentleness of a kindness she had not looked for.

On a clear, golden autumn morning the whole party agreed upon a long walk to Winthrop, a farm some miles away, and Anne was invited to join them. Mary, who preferred to be coaxed, declared that she would be quite exhausted long before they arrived, and set out regardless. Wentworth walked in front with the Musgrove sisters, and Anne took her place at the back.

Anne walked slowly at the rear of the party, enjoying, in spite of herself, the soft yellow light and the faded glory of the hedgerows. She was fond of autumn, with its gentle melancholy, and she thought of the poets who had written about the sweetness of a year that is passing. It was a kind of peace, and she had not had so much of it since the day that Wentworth came.

The party came to a hedge hanging thick with ripe nuts, and a quarrel of cheerful voices broke out as everyone began to pick. Anne, who was tired of the walk and tired of her own thoughts, sat down upon a bank behind the hedge, hidden from view. She had no wish to listen to others, but it was impossible not to hear the voices that came through the leaves.

The voices on the other side of the hedge were those of Wentworth and Louisa, and Wentworth was speaking with unusual earnestness. He had found a bright, perfect nut, which had weathered every storm of the season, and he said that a firm mind was like such a nut, strong and glossy and entire. Anne, who could see no more than the shadow of his coat, felt every word go through her.

Louisa answered that she would never allow herself to be persuaded into anything she did not believe, whatever her friends might say, and she spoke with the unbending confidence of a very young woman. Wentworth praised her for it and said that such firmness was the quality he valued above all others in a woman. Anne, listening in silence on the other side of the hedge, understood that she had just been condemned by implication, and that the verdict was a heavy one.

Anne could not be sure that the speech was aimed at her, but she felt it wounding her as surely as if it had been. She had let herself be persuaded, eight years before, and he had plainly never forgiven her for it, and he now rewarded the opposite quality in a younger woman. She rose from the bank, trembling a little, and walked on along the lane without making the smallest sound, so that nobody should know that she had heard.

Mary had been tiring for the last half mile, and at last she sat down upon a stile and announced that she could go no farther, whatever anyone might say. Charles tried first to coax her and then to scold her, and the party stood in a helpless group about her. Anne, who had never felt so tired in her life, leaned upon a gate and said nothing at all.

While they were still debating what was to be done, the Crofts appeared along the lane in their small open carriage, Admiral Croft driving with great energy and his wife beside him. Mrs Croft, who was quick to see when a person was exhausted, offered Anne a seat without delay. Anne, with a great deal of gratitude, accepted it, and was lifted up beside her.

The Admiral, a splendid seaman but a careless coachman, nearly turned the carriage over into the ditch on two occasions, and each time he laughed at the near disaster. Mrs Croft, who plainly had experience of such moments, calmly put her hand upon the reins and guided the horse back into the middle of the road. Anne, watching with some amusement, thought that she had never seen so good a marriage.

As they drove, the Admiral chatted freely about his brother-in-law, whom he said was certainly paying court to one of the Musgrove girls. He was not sure which of the two it would be, nor, apparently, was Frederick himself, but the matter would be settled before Christmas. Anne listened with her eyes fixed on the road, and said as little as she could, and thanked him for the ride.

One evening Wentworth began to talk about his old friend Captain Harville, who had settled with his family at Lyme, on the south coast, some seventeen miles from Uppercross. The Musgrove girls, who had hardly ever seen the sea, begged to be taken there at once, and their enthusiasm was too lively to be ignored. Even Charles and Mary agreed, after a short discussion about the roads and the expense, that it would be an excellent adventure for them all.

The party set off early on a cold November morning, a little crowd of six, muffled in coats and rugs and rattling along the narrow road toward the sea. Charles and Mary led the way, with Anne and the two Musgrove sisters in the second carriage, and Wentworth rode alongside, now ahead and now behind. Mary found the weather too cold and the roads too rough, but nobody else was at all inclined to listen.

After some hours of travelling they came down a steep, narrow street into the old town of Lyme, and the whole bay opened before them, grey-blue, wide and shining under a pale sky. The cliffs curved away on either side, the waves broke in long white lines, and the smell of salt water came through the carriage window. Anne, who loved the sea, drew in her breath and felt her troubles drop a little away.

The party engaged rooms at a modest inn close to the sea, and, after a hurried meal, wandered out to see the sights of the town. The great curve of the Cobb, a high stone wall that shelters the harbour from the weather, was the first thing that Anne wished to see. She walked along it slowly, with the wind in her face, and felt, for the first time in weeks, quite entirely at ease.

Wentworth led the way to a small house on the quay, where Captain Harville had taken a few rooms for himself and his family. The Captain, a tall, dark man with a thoughtful face, was lame from a wound that he had received two years earlier, and he welcomed the strangers with such open warmth that the smallness of the house was soon forgotten. Every inch of it, Anne noticed with growing admiration, had been arranged with the careful ingenuity of a man who had spent his life in ships.

Captain Harville, who could not walk far because of his lame leg, had filled his days with useful craft, and the little rooms were full of shelves, boxes and cupboards that he had made himself. He pointed out each one with a boyish pride, observing that a sailor learns early to make the most of a very small space. Anne thought that she had never seen so much cleverness or so much cheer in so little room.

The Harvilles would not hear of anyone leaving before dinner, and the whole party was squeezed into the narrow dining room, somewhat to the surprise of the cook. Mrs Harville, a calm, kind woman, offered each guest a share of what she had, and the Captain made them all laugh with his stories. Anne observed the affection of these naval friends for one another, and it moved her more deeply than she cared to say.

In a corner of the room sat Captain Benwick, a pale, quiet young officer dressed entirely in black, whom the Harvilles had taken into their house out of kindness. He had been engaged to the Captain's sister Fanny, and she had died the previous summer while he was far away at sea. His grief had not lessened with time, and he sat with a book in his hand and a face of settled sorrow.

After dinner Captain Benwick, who seemed to have found in Anne a sympathetic listener, walked with her along the beach and spoke at length of poetry. He knew the best-loved works of the day by heart, and he recited the mournful lines with a trembling voice, and his eyes were fixed upon the waves. Anne, who was patient and kind, let him talk and thought that he had not yet learned how to be consoled.

Anne, who felt a real pity for his condition, suggested very gently that too much poetry of that mournful kind might feed a sorrow rather than heal it. She recommended a course of good prose, with letters, lives and moral writings, which might steady his mind and lead him gradually back into the world. Benwick received her advice with surprise and then gratitude, and said that nobody had spoken so wisely to him since his loss.

Early the next morning Anne and the Musgrove sisters walked down to the beach, where the tide was coming in over the wet sand and the light lay bright upon the waves. The keen sea air brought a glow to Anne's cheeks that had not been seen for years, and she looked, in that clear morning, almost as pretty as she had been at nineteen. She was far too occupied with the beauty of the view to notice the change in herself, though other people did.

A gentleman passed them on the sand, and he looked at Anne with such frank and unconcealed admiration that she coloured even before she understood why. Wentworth, who was walking a few paces behind, saw the glance as plainly as she did, and for a moment his eyes rested upon her face as if he had never properly looked at it. It was a quick, unreadable look, but Anne felt it down to her heart.

The look that Wentworth gave her seemed to say, as clearly as speech, that he had noticed the return of her bloom and that he approved of it. He said nothing, and a moment later he was talking to Louisa about the tide, but the glance stayed in Anne's mind for the rest of the morning. She was angry with herself for noticing it, and she could not help being pleased.

Back at the inn Anne caught sight of the same stranger, who was standing beside a carriage while a servant strapped on the luggage. She saw that he wore a band of black upon his sleeve, as one in mourning, and he raised his hat as she passed, with a manner so well-bred that she could not doubt his rank. A moment later the carriage had rolled up the hill, and she had forgotten him.

The whole party walked up on the Cobb that afternoon, and Louisa, who had been seized with a fit of daring, insisted upon jumping down the high steps into the arms of Wentworth. He caught her laughing, set her on the pavement, and received her thanks with a smile that seemed to promise more than he meant. Anne, who stood a little way off with the others, kept a calm face and looked steadily at the sea.

Louisa, flushed with success, declared that she must jump again, from the higher flight, this time without any help at all. Wentworth, who knew a good deal about falls on a hard surface, begged her to be sensible, and said that the stones were unforgiving and the steps far too high. Louisa, who prided herself upon her firmness, only laughed, and ran up the steps again.

Louisa did not wait for the warning to end, and she leaped from the top of the steps before Wentworth had braced himself to receive her. He stretched out both arms and was a fraction of a second too slow, and she struck the paving with a dreadful sound. The whole party stood frozen on the wall for an instant, as if the world itself had stopped turning.

Louisa lay perfectly motionless upon the paving, her eyes closed and her face as white as marble, and Wentworth threw himself on his knees beside her. He took her in his arms and cried aloud, in a voice that none of them would ever forget, that she was dead. His face was quite changed with terror, and he looked at the others as if for help.

Mary shrieked and sank to the ground in a fit of hysterics, Henrietta fainted outright and fell against Anne's arm, and Charles stood staring at his sister as if he had lost his senses. Wentworth, still on his knees beside the girl, looked up and asked in an anguished voice whether nobody would help him. For one terrible moment, while the wind blew and the gulls cried above the harbour, no one moved or spoke.

Anne, who had been holding Henrietta, was the only one who kept her head, and her quiet voice rang out above the shrieks with surprising authority. She told Charles to go to Wentworth's side and help, and she turned to Captain Benwick, who had come running from the quay, and begged him to bring a surgeon without a moment's loss. In the confusion of that dreadful hour, and to the surprise of everyone including herself, the whole company obeyed her at once.

The scream had drawn a crowd of fishermen and townspeople to the Cobb, and the little group of visitors found themselves the centre of anxious stares. Captain Harville arrived at a limping run, took one look at the girl's white face, and at once took command, helping Wentworth to raise her gently from the stones. She was still breathing, though very faintly, but she gave no other sign of life, and her eyes remained closed.

Four strong men laid Louisa upon a plank and carried her through the steep, narrow streets of Lyme toward Captain Harville's house, with Wentworth walking at her head and refusing to be parted from her. Anne followed behind, supporting the trembling Henrietta, and the whole procession moved slowly and silently up the hill. The townspeople drew back from their doorways and looked on in a respectful silence, and many of them wept for the girl.

The surgeon, a grave, plain-spoken man, examined Louisa for a long time and at length declared that the blow to her head was a severe one, though not, in his judgement, a fatal one. She would need weeks of absolute quiet and constant care, and nobody could say for certain how her recovery would go. After the anguish of the afternoon, even this guarded hope seemed like a gift.

Mrs Harville, without a moment's hesitation, insisted that Louisa should remain in her own house, where she and a skilled nurse of her acquaintance could attend to her night and day. The rooms were already crowded with her own children and Captain Benwick, but not a word of complaint escaped any of the family. Anne marvelled at the generosity of people who had so little to give and gave it so freely.

Mary announced, between her sobs, that she was quite determined to remain at Lyme and nurse Louisa herself, and that Anne, who was not even a Musgrove, should go home in her place. Anne, who would have been far better at the work and knew it, did not argue, since a quarrel would only have added to the confusion. She bowed her head and agreed, with the quiet obedience of long habit, to do exactly as she was told.

Wentworth drew Anne aside, and spoke in a low and urgent voice, saying that somebody must carry the dreadful news to Mr and Mrs Musgrove and that it must be done with great gentleness. There was no one else who could do it so well, he said, and he begged her to be the one. It was the first time in eight years that he had asked her for anything.

Wentworth hurried out and hired a closed carriage, and when it stood ready at the door, he handed Anne in with an attention that she could not mistake. He looked at her for a moment, as though he wished to say something large and could find no words, and then he stepped back and gave the order to start. She watched him standing in the road until the street turned a corner and he passed out of her sight.

The journey home was long, dark and almost silent, for Henrietta wept quietly in her corner and Charles stared out of the window without a word. Anne held the weeping girl's hand and tried to find the words in which the dreadful tidings should be told to her parents. All the while, in the hidden part of her mind, she saw Wentworth's face as it had looked at the carriage door.

Anne told the parents what had happened with all the gentleness she could command, and the old couple received the news with tears and trembling and a great deal of useless exclamation. Mrs Musgrove, who was already a mother in motion, packed a bundle and set out for Lyme within the hour, while her husband walked about the house in a daze. Anne, who was left at Uppercross to keep the children, was asked to look after everything.

A few weeks later, while Louisa was slowly mending at Lyme under the care of the Harvilles, Lady Russell arrived at Uppercross and embraced Anne with unusual warmth. She had come to carry her friend away to Bath, where the family was waiting, and Anne, who had been useful to everybody for two months, was suddenly released. She said her farewells to the cottage and the Musgroves, and left with a heart that was full and confused.

On the long road to Bath Lady Russell studied Anne's face with satisfaction and declared that she was greatly improved, with more colour, more spirit and something of her old bloom. She credited the sea air at Lyme with the change, and Anne let her believe it, for she could not very well explain the real cause. It was strange, she thought, how little a face could keep a secret from those who loved it and looked at it so closely.

They drove into Bath through a heavy and steady rain, and the whole city lay half hidden in smoke and mist, its pale houses rising in rows up the hill. Lady Russell, who had lived there before, was glad to be among familiar streets, but Anne, who dreaded the crowds and the noise, longed for the hedges and the quiet of the country. She could not tell yet whether she would ever learn to like the place, though she meant to try very hard.

Lady Russell had taken a comfortable house in Rivers Street, within a short walk of the Elliots' lodgings, and she settled herself in it with the calm of a person who is perfectly at home. She was glad to have Anne near her, and she had already formed many plans for her friend's future, none of which was ever mentioned until they were ready. Anne, who knew her friend very well, waited with some alarm and a little amusement to learn what they were.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth had taken a tall, dignified house in Camden Place, in the finest part of Bath, and they led Anne through every room with the pride of a pair who had won a prize. Folding doors, handsome furniture and a view of the hills were all pointed out to her in turn, and each was said to be far superior to anything at Kellynch. They did not once ask how Louisa Musgrove was, or whether anyone had been hurt at Lyme, or how Anne herself had borne it.

Elizabeth, who had grown more elegant and more cold during the weeks in Bath, talked without pause about her parties and her acquaintances and the noble families whose cards lay upon the table. Nobody asked Anne about Uppercross or the accident at Lyme or anything that had happened in her own life. She listened politely and understood that she was still, to her own family, a convenient and silent piece of furniture.

Mrs Clay was still in residence, as warm and agreeable as ever, and Anne noticed at once with misgiving how sweetly she smiled upon Sir Walter. She laughed at his jokes, she admired his opinions, and she managed to be at his elbow whenever a cup of tea or a chair was wanted. Anne, who had seen the same thing at Kellynch, wondered whether anyone, even Lady Russell, could be made to take the danger seriously.

Sir Walter, who observed the streets of Bath from his window like a general studying the field, told Anne that there was a lamentable number of plain faces in the town. He had once counted fifty ugly women in the course of a single walk, and he doubted very much whether there was a handsome man to be seen. He would not have said it so confidently, perhaps, if he had remembered the mirrors.

The thing that occupied the Elliots most at that time was their relation to Lady Dalrymple, a dowager viscountess who lived in Laura Place. She had a daughter, Miss Carteret, who was as dull as herself, and neither lady possessed the smallest charm or intelligence. Both possessed a title, however, and Sir Walter and Elizabeth pursued the acquaintance with a patience that they had never shown in any other cause.

Sir Walter then spoke about his cousin and heir, Mr William Elliot, who would inherit the baronetcy when Sir Walter died, and who had behaved for many years in a manner that Sir Walter considered quite improper. He had kept away from the family, he had married a rich woman of no name, and he had spoken lightly of the title that he was to inherit. Now, however, he was a widower with a large fortune and a good deal of leisure, and he wished very much to be forgiven.

The next day Mr Elliot himself called at Camden Place, a tall, handsome, well-dressed man of about thirty-five with the grace of a perfect courtier. He bowed to Sir Walter, expressed his deep regret at the long silence between them, and begged to be forgiven in terms so elegant that nobody could refuse him. Sir Walter was delighted, Elizabeth was flattered, and even Anne could not find fault with his manners.

Mr Elliot explained his long silence with great skill, saying that he had been a thoughtless young man, anxious to make his way in the world and careless of the claims of his family. He now regretted it sincerely, and he said so in such measured, sensible terms that Sir Walter was entirely charmed. Anne, who watched him from her chair by the fire, thought that she had never met a man who spoke so well.

As Mr Elliot turned toward the window, the light fell full upon his face, and Anne suddenly recognised him with a start. He was the very gentleman who had stared at her with such open admiration on the beach at Lyme and who had later been seen stepping into a carriage at the inn. She said nothing at the time, but the discovery was a considerable surprise, and it set her thoughts moving at once.

Mr Elliot, who evidently saw that she had recognised him, bowed to her gravely and confessed that he had admired her at Lyme without knowing who she was. He said that he was delighted to find her a cousin and that he hoped to know her a great deal better. Anne blushed and murmured a reply, and was pleased in spite of herself, for it had been a long time since a man had spoken so to her.

Mr Elliot dined at Camden Place on several evenings in the following week, and on each occasion he seated himself near Anne and spoke to her with growing ease and attention. He praised her good sense, her taste in music and her gentle way with the old, and Anne, who was not used to compliments, found them a pleasant change. She began, against her expectation, to think him an excellent companion, and she looked forward a little to the hour of his arrival.

Lady Russell was introduced to Mr Elliot soon afterward and found him everything that a gentleman should be: polite, reasonable, well-informed and wealthy, with exactly the correct opinions upon every subject. She could see at a glance why he had made such a favourable impression on the family. Before the evening was over, an idea that she had never before dared to entertain had begun to form in her mind.

Lady Russell began to dream that Anne might one day marry Mr Elliot and become mistress of Kellynch Hall, wearing the title that her own mother had worn. How satisfying it would be, she thought, to see the rightful daughter in the rightful home, and she dropped a few gentle hints. Anne listened with polite attention and offered no answer, which was, to Lady Russell, a promising sign.

Anne found that, on the whole, she liked Mr Elliot, and yet she could not wholly trust him. He was always rational, always correct and always agreeable, and she had never once seen him angry, enthusiastic or in any way off his guard. A man so perfectly polished, she thought, might be hiding a good deal behind the surface.

One morning, in a shop doorway, Anne met her old governess, who told her that her best friend at school, Miss Hamilton, was living in Bath. The girl was now Mrs Smith, a widow of some years' standing, who had been left poor and was now lame with rheumatic fever. Anne, who remembered her as the kindest of her companions, resolved to visit her at once.

Anne walked the length of a dingy street to a poor and crowded corner of Bath called Westgate Buildings, and climbed a narrow staircase to two small rooms at the top. There she found her old friend, thin and lame and surrounded by few comforts, her once pretty face lined with long suffering. For a moment Anne was too moved to speak, and she could only hold out both her hands to the friend of her girlhood.

Mrs Smith received her old friend with such a bright smile and such a cheerful heart that Anne soon forgot the dingy rooms and the poor furniture. She did not complain of her poverty or her pain, and she spoke warmly of her kind nurse, Mrs Rooke, who looked after her every day. Anne marvelled at her courage, and understood that happiness has little to do with fortune.

Anne mentioned, at dinner, that she had been visiting an old school friend who lived in Westgate Buildings, and she was astonished at the effect of her words. Elizabeth lifted her chin in horror, and Sir Walter observed in a voice of deep reproach that no daughter of his ought to be seen in such a quarter. Anne answered quietly that she was going to see a friend and not the street.

Not long afterward there was a fashionable evening party at Camden Place, and Anne, who had no great taste for such occasions, quietly asked to be excused so that she might sit with Mrs Smith. Elizabeth could hardly believe her ears, and Sir Walter asked whether she preferred a sick woman to the best company in Bath. Anne said that she did, and she walked out into the evening feeling happier than she had been all week.

Mrs Smith showed Anne the little knitted articles that she made and sold to earn a trifle, and she described the humours of her narrow life with real wit. She had learned, she said, to find pleasure in small things, in a kind visit, a good book or a lively tale, and she bore her illness as a soldier bears a long campaign. Anne left her that evening humbled and strengthened at once, and she walked home thinking how little the lack of money had to do with joy.

A long, rambling letter arrived from Mary, full of her own aches and griefs but carrying news of real interest at the end. Louisa was now sitting up, though still weak, and the surgeon expected that in time she would entirely recover, and be able to travel. Anne read it twice with a thankful heart, folded it carefully, and then laid it down upon the table beside her.

Mary also added, in her careless way, that Captain Benwick had become a constant visitor at the Harvilles' and seemed to spend most of every day beside Louisa's sofa, reading aloud to her. Louisa, it appeared, did not object, and Mary thought it was great fun to see a sad young man and a lively young woman so busy with each other. Mary could not guess how it would end, and nor, at that distance, could Anne, though she thought of Wentworth at once.

That same month Admiral and Mrs Croft arrived in Bath, the Admiral having been plagued by a troublesome gout that the waters were expected to relieve. They took lodgings near Camden Place and called at once on the family whose house they rented, in the genuine hope of being kind. Anne, who had always liked them, was very glad to see two friendly faces in a town where she had so few.

In the drawing room the Admiral leaned toward Anne and told her, with great relish, an astonishing piece of news. Miss Louisa Musgrove, it appeared, was to be married not to Frederick Wentworth, as the whole neighbourhood had expected, but to young Captain Benwick, who had lost his heart while nursing her. The old man was cheerfully amazed, and Anne, for a moment, forgot how to breathe.

Anne understood in an instant that Wentworth was not engaged and had never been, and a great wave of joy and fear went through her. She bent her face over her work so that nobody should see the colour in it, and she answered the Admiral in what she hoped was a quiet and ordinary tone. The room, which had seemed so dull a minute before, seemed to have grown wonderfully bright and warm.

Mrs Croft, who spoke more softly than her husband, told Anne that her brother had behaved with perfect honour throughout the sad business and that he was entirely free to choose again. She believed he would be glad of it, though she added with a smile that Frederick never said what he felt. Anne, who had learned that lesson long ago, said nothing, and her heart beat harder.

Mr Elliot called at Camden Place a few days later and told Anne that he was obliged, to his great regret, to leave Bath for a day or two on business of his own. He lingered over his farewell, took her hand with some feeling and begged her not to forget him in his absence. Anne smiled and said that she would not, and found, with some surprise, that she was pleased to see him go.

Anne was walking along Milsom Street on a damp and crowded morning when, quite suddenly, the face she most wanted and most feared to see appeared among the umbrellas. Captain Wentworth had arrived in Bath only the day before, and he stood within a few feet of her, looking thinner, graver and more handsome than ever. For a moment neither of them moved, and the crowd flowed round them like a river round two stones.

Wentworth crossed the pavement, bowed to her, and began to speak with a stiff and awkward courtesy that was clearly the result of some inner struggle. He asked after her health, spoke of Louisa's engagement with an air of pleasant surprise and added that he considered Benwick a lucky man. Anne answered each remark as well as she could, and her voice, she was glad to find, did not shake.

Lady Russell, driving along the street in her carriage, noticed Anne in earnest conversation with a tall man in a naval coat and asked who he was. When Anne told her, she looked at him long and critically, and then said, rather unexpectedly, that he was far better looking than she had remembered. It was, in fact, the nearest that Lady Russell would ever come to an apology for her opinion of eight years before.

Not many days later the Musgroves descended upon Bath in force, with Mrs Musgrove, Mary, Charles and Henrietta, together with Charles Hayter, in a long procession of luggage. They took rooms at the White Hart, an old inn in the middle of the town, where Mrs Musgrove wanted to buy wedding clothes, Mary wanted to be amused, and everybody wanted to see the shops. Anne called on them that same afternoon, and was received with a warmth that surprised her and a great many questions about Bath.

Anne found the whole family in excellent spirits, for Henrietta was now publicly engaged to her cousin Charles Hayter, and nobody remembered that she had once been fascinated by Captain Wentworth. The young couple glowed with a quiet and settled content that needed no explanation, and they hardly noticed anyone else in the room. Mrs Musgrove spoke of the wedding with the air of a woman ordering a ship, and Anne congratulated them all warmly.

A day later Mr Elliot returned from his journey and, meeting Anne in the street, walked home beside her with an arm offered and a smile bestowed. Across the road, among the crowd, Wentworth saw them together, and he drew from the sight the conclusion that Anne's heart was quite engaged. Anne, who saw him only for a moment, was not aware of the effect she was having.

Mary, who could never keep a piece of gossip to herself, informed Anne that the whole of Bath was talking of her coming marriage to Mr Elliot. Captain Wentworth, she added with a certain relish, had certainly heard it, since the Musgroves' acquaintance had been telling it for a week. Anne protested that there was no truth in it, and Mary replied that she had better say so soon.

That night Anne lay awake for hours, turning over every word she had spoken and every word she wished she had spoken. She could not go to Wentworth and explain, for a woman has no right to begin such conversations, and he, who might have begun them, was proud and angry and perhaps no longer interested. The silence between them seemed as thick and as high as a wall, and she could see no door in it.

Mr Elliot called again at Camden Place and made it known that he intended to be Anne's escort at the great concert in the Octagon Room, which the whole party was to attend. Lady Russell approved the arrangement, Sir Walter approved it, and there was nothing in all the world that Anne could find to say against it. She promised with as good a grace as she could manage, and then sat down alone to dread the evening.

When Anne next visited Westgate Buildings, Mrs Smith, who saw more from her chair than most women saw from the best windows in Bath, studied her face and put a very direct question. She wished to know whether Miss Elliot was indeed engaged to marry Mr William Elliot, since the rumour had reached even her little room. Anne laughed, flushed and said that there was no such thing, and Mrs Smith looked deeply relieved.

Mrs Smith, relieved to hear that no engagement existed, hesitated a moment and then spoke out with the gravity of a woman who has a painful duty to perform. She said that Mr Elliot was a cold, calculating man who had never in his life loved anything but his own comfort, and she begged Anne to hear her story before she trusted him. Anne, who was astonished and a good deal alarmed, sat down beside her friend's chair and prepared to listen.

Many years before, Mrs Smith explained, when she was newly married and comfortably rich, Mr Elliot had been the closest friend of her husband and a constant guest at their table. He was poor then, and he borrowed freely from Mr Smith, who was generous and trusting and never thought to ask for a repayment. They had seen him almost every day, and she had believed him to be a true friend.

In those days, said Mrs Smith, Mr Elliot spoke of his family with ill-concealed contempt, and he laughed at the idea of the baronetcy, which he said he would gladly sell for a small sum. He thought of money as the only real thing in the world, and he valued friendship exactly in proportion to what it could give him. She had been young enough then, and gay enough, to find his bitter wit amusing, and she blamed herself for it now.

Not long afterward Mr Elliot made a marriage with a rich woman of low birth, for no other reason than her fortune, and he let it be seen that he had no further need of his old friends. He ceased to visit the Smiths, he ceased to write to them, and he left them to their own devices without a word of farewell. It was soon after this unkind withdrawal that her husband's troubles began, and they did not end until the day he died.

Mr Smith, who had spent far more than he could afford and had trusted too many people, soon lost the greater part of his fortune, and with it his health. He died after a long illness, leaving his wife with almost nothing but debts and a weak body. Within a few years she was living in two rooms in Westgate Buildings, and she had no one to turn to.

Before he died, Mr Smith had named his old friend as the person to settle his affairs and take care of his widow, in the belief that no gentleman could refuse such a trust. Mr Elliot refused to act, did not so much as answer the letters that she wrote to him, and left her to struggle alone. It was a piece of coldness, she said, that she could never forget or forgive.

Mr Smith, Mrs Smith went on, had also owned property in the West Indies, which might be recovered with a little legal help, and which would have been enough to give her a comfortable income. A word from Mr Elliot, who knew all about it, would have put the affair right. He had declined to say that word, and she lived on, patiently, in poverty.

There was one thing more, said Mrs Smith, and that was the reason she had spoken at all. Her nurse, Mrs Rooke, who attended a certain lady in the fashionable part of Bath, had heard from that lady's husband, a close friend of Mr Elliot, a surprising account of his present purposes. She wished Anne to know it before the concert, since she feared that Anne might otherwise be deceived to her lasting cost.

Mr Elliot, Mrs Smith said, was alarmed by the attentions that Mrs Clay paid to Sir Walter, for a second marriage and a son would rob him of the baronetcy that he had once despised and now eagerly desired. He had therefore returned to the family, made himself agreeable to Anne and put himself on a footing to watch every move. A marriage with Anne would secure him, besides, the best of all possible positions, at the very side of the house whose name he hoped to inherit.

Anne sat for some moments without a word, feeling the foundations of her recent opinion give way, and then she thanked her friend with real feeling for her honesty and her courage. She promised to do whatever she could to help to recover the property in the West Indies, and she walked home slowly, with her mind in a whirl. Everything that she had half felt and half feared about Mr Elliot now made perfect sense, and she wondered at her own blindness.

That evening Mr Elliot arrived at Camden Place in the most elegant of evening clothes, with a smile for Sir Walter and a gracious word for Elizabeth, and Anne watched him as she might have watched a stranger. She was polite, she was calm, and she listened to his charming remarks with an inner ear that heard the cold voice that Mrs Smith had described. It was a very odd feeling, she thought, to be deceived no longer by a man whom everybody else admired so much.

The Elliot party travelled to the Octagon Room in a procession of chairs and carriages, through streets bright with lamps and loud with the hum of fashionable people. The concert was the great event of the Bath season, and everyone who counted themselves anyone was arriving to be seen. Anne, with Lady Russell at her side, followed her father and sister into the building with a heart that was far from the music.

The Octagon Room was crowded to the doors with elegant ladies in white and gentlemen in fine coats, and the candles hung in glittering rings over their heads. Sir Walter and Elizabeth pushed through the crowd to find their grand relation Lady Dalrymple, while Anne, with a quiet and persistent eagerness, looked along every row for a tall figure in a naval coat. She did not see him at first, and she hid her disappointment behind a polite and fashionable smile.

Wentworth arrived at last, rather late, in the company of a party from the White Hart, and stood for a moment at the end of the room searching the faces. When his eyes found Anne's, he seemed to hesitate, and then he made his way slowly toward her through the crowd, with a look that she could not quite read. She stood very still, and the music of the orchestra seemed to fade away into a distant and meaningless hum.

Wentworth stood beside Anne's chair and spoke of Captain Benwick and Louisa, confessing that he had been astonished by the match, since a sad and bookish man and a lively, spirited girl seemed so ill-suited to each other. Anne answered with gentle good humour, and for the first time in eight years their talk was nearly easy. She felt, as she listened to him, as if a door that had been shut for eight years had opened a very little.

At that moment Mr Elliot approached and, with a charming smile, asked Anne to help him with the Italian words printed upon the programme, since he said that nobody translated so well. She obliged, with a polite face and an unquiet mind, and he drew his chair closer to hers in order to follow her explanation. Over his shoulder, from across the crowded room, she could feel Wentworth's eyes resting upon them both with a cold attention.

Mr Elliot bent his head close to Anne's to catch her words, and he murmured something about the sweetness of the name Elliot, which she was too much distracted to hear. A few feet away Wentworth stood stiff and silent, his face growing darker with every moment, as if he were watching a thing that he had foreseen. Anne turned toward Wentworth in dismay, hoping to explain with a glance, but by then it was far too late.

Wentworth said, in a voice very different from the one he had used a few minutes earlier, that he must leave, since the music was not much to his taste. He bowed to Anne with the most distant courtesy, turned on his heel, and walked out through the crowd before she could find a word to stop him. The door closed behind him, and for Anne the whole brilliant room seemed suddenly empty, as though the lights had been put out.

Anne remained in her seat through the long second half of the concert, with her hands folded and her eyes fixed on the singers, and she did not hear a single note of the music. She had been given one chance in eight years to speak, and she had lost it to an evening of translation. The whole bright and glittering room might as well have been a desert, for all the pleasure it gave her.

On the drive back to Camden Place, Anne, sitting silent in a corner of the carriage while Mr Elliot talked pleasantly of the evening, made up her mind. Whatever the cost to her pride, she would go to the White Hart in the morning, among the Musgroves, and there find some way of letting Wentworth see that he was mistaken. She had been too quiet for too long, and she told herself that eight years of silence were quite enough.

The next morning Anne walked briskly through the bright streets toward the White Hart, and her heart beat so quickly that she was obliged to slow her pace. She had decided in the night to be bold, and she meant to keep that resolution in the daylight, whatever it might cost her. Twice she nearly turned back in the street, and twice she lifted her chin, drew a deep breath and walked on.

In the large sitting room at the White Hart Mrs Musgrove received Anne with delight, led her to a seat by the window and began to talk at great length about wedding clothes. She described the ribbons she had seen, the prices she had paid and the shops she meant to visit, and she required no answer but an occasional nod. Anne, who was thinking of something else entirely and listening for a single voice, supplied the nods in the proper places.

At the far end of the room, with his back half turned, Wentworth sat writing at a small desk, and he rose to bow to Anne with the greatest formality before sitting down again. He seemed wholly occupied with his pen, and Anne, sitting at the window beside Mrs Musgrove, could not tell whether he knew that she was there. She did not dare to look at him directly, though every nerve in her body was aware of him.

Captain Harville arrived at the inn that morning, having come to Bath on business of his own, and he sat down beside Anne at the window with the easy friendliness of an old acquaintance. They began to talk in low voices of Lyme, of the children and of Louisa's progress, and Anne, in spite of everything, felt her spirits begin to rise a little. It was pleasant, in the middle of so much anxiety, to speak with someone who was honest and plain and kind.

Captain Harville took from his pocket a small portrait of Captain Benwick, which had been painted for his sister Fanny at the Cape of Good Hope and which he had now been asked to have reset for another lady. He held it in his hand and looked at it for a moment with a tight and troubled face. It was clear to Anne that the commission gave him no pleasure, and that he would gladly have been rid of it.

Captain Harville said, with a sigh, that his poor sister Fanny would never have transferred her love in six months, and he supposed that it was the way of the world. Men, he declared, were the more constant of the two sexes, and he cited as proof the proverbs, the songs and the stories that every one of them had heard. Anne, who had been listening quietly with her hands in her lap, felt her colour rising and her courage with it.

Anne replied, with more spirit than she knew she possessed, that she would not allow any book as evidence in the matter. All the stories had been told by men, she said, and men had always possessed every advantage in education and the use of the pen. She did not think the dispute could fairly be settled by one side alone, and Captain Harville, who had not expected an argument from so quiet a person, smiled with surprise.

Anne said, in a low and steady voice, that if there was any privilege belonging to her sex, it was that of loving longest, when existence or hope had passed away. She added that women could not help it, since their lives were quiet and their feelings had little else to occupy them, and she spoke with a depth that held the room's attention. Her eyes were very bright, her cheeks were glowing, and her hands were pressed tightly together in her lap.

Captain Harville answered gently that sailors felt every bit as deeply as the sex that stayed at home. He described, with a rough tenderness, the grief of a man who must leave his wife and children for a long voyage, and Anne said that she did not for a moment doubt it. Her only claim, she added, was that women's lives allowed their feelings to last a little longer, and it was a quiet disagreement between two honest people.

Behind them there was a sudden small noise, and when Anne turned, she saw that Wentworth had let his pen fall to the floor. He had heard every word, and for a moment he looked at her with a face so full of feeling that she could hardly bear it, and then he rose and walked quickly out of the room. The door closed softly behind him, and in the silence that followed Anne could hear her own heart beating.

Anne sat perfectly still, with her pulse racing and her thoughts in a whirl, and the sounds of the room seemed to come from a very long way off. Mrs Musgrove went happily on about her ribbons and her prices, and Captain Harville returned to the window, and Anne understood nothing that was said to her. She was waiting, though she hardly knew for what, and she was conscious only of a great and growing hope.

A few minutes later Wentworth returned, saying that he had left his gloves behind, and he went to the desk, where he made some small movement among the papers. He looked at Anne for a moment with a face that said a hundred things, and then he left the room again as swiftly as he had come. The whole visit lasted less than a minute, and Mrs Musgrove, who was busy with a sleeve, never even looked up.

Captain Harville went across to the desk, looked down, and saw a folded letter lying there with the direction written in a hurried hand: it was addressed to Miss A E, and the writing was Wentworth's. He picked it up and put it into Anne's hand without a word, with a smile of understanding that was kind and quiet. Anne's fingers trembled so much that she could hardly hold the paper, and she turned toward the window for the light.

Anne unfolded the letter and read it slowly, through eyes that were already blurring, while the voices of the room faded entirely. Wentworth wrote that he could no longer remain silent, that her words to Captain Harville had pierced him to the soul, and that he hardly knew whether he was in pain or in hope. She read it three times over before she could believe it, and each time her heart beat faster than before.

Wentworth wrote that he had loved no one but her in all those long years, that he had been unjust, resentful and weak, but that he had never once been inconstant. He begged her to forgive him, if she could, and said that if her feelings were what he now dared to hope, she had only to give him a word or a look. His handwriting shook a little as the lines went on, as though the writer had hardly been able to hold his pen.

Anne found that she could not hide her tears, and she stood up in some confusion, murmuring that she must go. Mrs Musgrove, who saw only a pale face and a trembling hand, cried out that poor Miss Elliot must be unwell, and offered her a chair and a glass of water. Anne declined both and managed to say that she wished only to be in the open air.

Charles Musgrove, who was on his way out, offered to walk with Anne as far as Camden Place, and she was glad of any escort that would not require her to speak. He chatted pleasantly of his dogs and his guns and the sad price of game in Bath. She answered him at random, with her heart full of one name and her ears full of another.

In the next street they met Wentworth, who had plainly been walking up and down in the hope of this very encounter, and his face as he approached was filled with a question. Charles, who suspected nothing, said that he had to go to the gunmaker's, and gladly handed Anne over to Wentworth's care. He departed whistling cheerfully down the street, and neither of them was aware of the moment that he went.

They walked together in silence for some minutes, through the streets and then along a quiet gravel path beside a row of high old trees, where no other person came. There Wentworth stopped, turned and spoke to her at last with his whole heart, as he had not spoken since the summer of 1806. She looked into his face, and she found there, plainly written, everything that she had thought lost for ever.

Wentworth told her, in plain and passionate words, that he had never stopped loving her for a single day, that he had tried in a hundred ways to forget her and failed in every one. Anne answered that her feelings had not changed in eight years, that she had loved only him and expected to love only him, and her voice broke. In that moment the whole long silence that had lain between them for eight years dissolved like mist in the sun.

Wentworth explained, with great frankness, that he had never loved Louisa Musgrove, whatever the neighbourhood supposed, and that his gallantry had been a way of avoiding his own thoughts. After the accident at Lyme, honour had seemed to bind him to her, and he had stayed where he was in an unhappy confusion. He had feared, for some weeks, that honour would compel him to marry her, and he had been miserable at the thought.

It was at Lyme, he told her, that his eyes were opened, for there he saw the difference between mere obstinacy and true strength of mind. Louisa's firmness had led to a fall, while Anne's had kept a whole terrified company steady, and every one of them had turned to her. He had understood in that dreadful hour that he had been looking for exactly what he had thrown away.

Wentworth admitted that he had been resentful for the greater part of eight years, and that he had longed to show her, and himself, that he could do without her. He had been hurt, he said, and he had mistaken his pride for strength, and he had wasted a great deal of time. It was a plain, honest speech, and Anne listened with eyes full of love.

Anne told him, with great gentleness, that she had believed herself right to be guided by Lady Russell, who had stood in the place of a mother to her. She had acted from duty and not from any lack of love, she said, and she would not have urged such a choice upon any other young woman, but she did not regret her obedience. Wentworth, who had listened without interruption, forgave her in a single word, and she knew that he meant it entirely.

Wentworth confessed that he had always held Lady Russell responsible, and that for years he had thought of her as an enemy, but that he now saw something of her side. He had been a young man without fortune and with no certain future, and she had had good reason to be afraid. He added, with a smile, that he was none the less glad that the matter had come out right.

Anne told him plainly that there had never been the slightest question of her marrying Mr Elliot, whatever the gossips of Bath supposed, and that she had come to distrust him entirely. Wentworth laughed with relief and confessed that he had walked out of the concert because he could not bear to see them together. He had not known until that night that he was capable of such jealousy, and he was a little ashamed of it.

The clouds had cleared while they talked, and the low sun was gilding the pale stone of the terraces and turning every puddle to gold. For the first time Anne thought the city of Bath beautiful, and she saw that the beauty had been there all the time, waiting for her eyes. She was too happy to say so aloud, and Wentworth, who walked beside her, was happy in the same silent way.

That evening Sir Walter had an evening party at Camden Place, and Wentworth came, at Anne's invitation, and was received by her father with a bow of unexpected civility. The baronet noticed with surprise that the penniless sailor of 1806 had become a handsome, well-dressed man of rank and fortune, and he found that he could not entirely despise him. Elizabeth, who had been prepared to be cold, found his manner so agreeable that she was gracious in return.

Lady Russell, from her place near the fire, watched Anne and Wentworth as they talked together in a corner, and she observed the new light in Anne's face and the tender attention in his. A glance was enough for a woman of her intelligence, and she felt, with some pain and a great deal of honesty, that her judgement of eight years before had been mistaken. She said nothing yet, but she resolved that she would speak to Anne before the evening was over, and speak honestly.

Mr Elliot, standing near the door with an expression of studied calm, read the whole story in Anne's radiant face, and understood that his chance was gone. He bowed to the company with perfect politeness, took his leave early, and walked out into the night with the manner of a man who is making new plans. Nobody noticed him go except the one person who had been warned, and she felt a quiet and thankful relief.

The next morning Wentworth called at Camden Place and asked Sir Walter, with correct and serious courtesy, for his daughter's hand. He was now a captain of honourable fame and handsome fortune, and the baronet, after a pause that was meant to preserve his dignity, gave a consent that he could not decently refuse. It was the first real favour that he had ever granted Anne in the whole course of her life.

Lady Russell took Anne's hand, and with a moisture in her own eyes that was rare in that composed woman, she admitted that she had misjudged Wentworth in every way eight years before. She had seen a poor young man with no prospects, she said, where she ought to have seen courage, talent and a loving heart. Anne forgave her at once, and embraced her with all her heart, and for a long time neither of them could speak.

Sir Walter, as soon as the engagement was certain, took down his favourite volume of the baronetage, found the page of his family, and entered the news of Anne's marriage in his best handwriting. He was entirely satisfied, since he could now write the name of an honourable and respected man beside his daughter's, and he did so with a smile of ceremonial pride. The book, he reflected, had never seemed so satisfactory, and he closed it with the air of a man at peace with the world.

Wentworth, who had many friends in the navy and a good deal of experience of the West Indies, helped Mrs Smith to recover her husband's property with the energy that he brought to everything, and her income was soon restored. She moved to a pleasanter home, gained new strength, and rejoiced to see her old friend so happy. Anne was glad to think that a little good had been done, and she said so to Wentworth that evening.

Soon afterward Mr Elliot left Bath, and within a few days it was discovered that Mrs Clay had left too and had put herself under his protection in London. Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and deeply mortified, and it was whispered that she had not, after all, won the title she wanted. The two schemers, it was agreed, had each been caught in the net that was meant for somebody else.

When Mary heard the news, she was delighted that her sister should have so rich and well-regarded a husband, though she could not entirely conceal a trace of jealousy. She observed that Anne would have a better carriage than she did, and she reminded the family that it was she who had first made the Captain welcome at Uppercross. Nobody argued with her, for it was easier to let her enjoy a little glory, and Anne smiled kindly and said nothing.

Admiral and Mrs Croft received the news with the heartiest delight, the Admiral shaking Wentworth's hand until the poor man winced and declaring that nothing could be better. Mrs Croft kissed Anne and said that she had always hoped that her brother might find a wife with real courage. The Musgroves, too, sent warm and noisy congratulations from Uppercross, and Charles wrote that he had always said the Captain was the finest fellow alive.

Anne and Wentworth were married soon afterward in a quiet ceremony, with Lady Russell, the Crofts and a small number of friends beside them. Anne wore a simple dress, and her face was lit with a happiness she had not known for eight years, and Wentworth could scarcely look at her without smiling. It was exactly the wedding that she would have chosen for herself, simple, affectionate and entirely free of show.

Anne gloried in being a sailor's wife, in the warmth of the Navy and the loyalty of its families, and she thought that no woman in England had a better husband or a better friend. Yet she knew that she must pay for such happiness with a constant quickness of alarm, for if war came again, he would go to sea, and she would wait at home. She accepted the price without a murmur, and counted it small beside the happiness that she had been given.

Anne and Wentworth stood together at the window one bright evening and watched a ship making its way far out upon the shining water. They had been parted by persuasion and brought together by constancy, and they had waited eight long years for this quiet moment, and it was worth every one of them. The sea lay wide and calm before them, and for that moment, at least, neither of them was afraid of anything.
